item.title: How big a tank does an aquatic turtle need?
item.description: The rule of thumb is about 10 gallons of water per inch of shell, and sliders grow fast enough that an adult can need 75 gallons or more. How to size the tank, why a plain storage tote is a good first one, and what else has to grow with it.
item.content:encoded:
Most new turtle keepers size the tank for the turtle they bring home. That is the trap. A hatchling looks lost in almost any container, so a small tank feels generous on day one, and nothing about it looks wrong until the turtle has quietly outgrown it.

The Smart Turtle Tank book opens its care chapter with exactly this, under a heading that sums it up: bigger than you think, sooner than you think. This post covers the sizing rule, what a sensible first tank looks like, and the parts of the setup that have to scale with the water.

One caveat, straight from the book: this is general guidance for aquatic turtles such as sliders. Your species may want different numbers, so check a care sheet written for it, and ask a reptile vet if anything looks off.

The rule: about 10 gallons per inch of shell

The rule of thumb for aquatic turtles is about 10 gallons of water per inch of shell. Note that it says water, not tank: a tank is never filled to the brim, and the dry dock takes up room too.

The arithmetic is simple enough to do with a ruler:

Shell lengthWater to plan for
2 inchesabout 20 gallons
4 inchesabout 40 gallons
6 inchesabout 60 gallons

The second half of the rule is the part that catches people. A hatchling is fine in a small tank for a while, but sliders grow fast, and an adult can need 75 gallons or more. A tank that is right today has an expiry date, and the turtle sets it, not you.

The trap: waiting for the turtle to tell you

The usual way people find out a tank is too small is that the turtle runs out of room to swim. The book's answer is to keep a clock instead. Its turtle cam includes an age counter that shows days, then weeks and days, and the book calls it the "time for a bigger tank" clock. The point is to know when the small tank stops being enough before the turtle has to show you.

You do not need a camera app for this. A note of the date the turtle arrived, plus a shell measurement now and then, does the same job: multiply the shell length by 10 and compare it to the water you actually have.

A good first tank can be a storage tote

The book's own first tank is a clear plastic storage tote. It sounds cheap because it is, and the book still calls it a very good first tank:

  • It is light.
  • It does not crack.
  • It is easy to drain into the sink, which matters for weekly water changes.
  • Its rim is a flat lip that printed parts can grip, which is how the book's sensor build hangs its probe hook and electronics box on the tank.

The one thing to get right when you pick a tote: choose one that is longer than it is tall. Turtles swim sideways and climb out upward. Floor length is swimming room; height mostly gives a determined turtle something to climb.

If you would rather buy a kit, the book notes that pet stores sell turtle starter kits (it found a 20-gallon one with the lamp fixtures and bulbs, a thermometer, a floating dock, gravel and food). The kit route is the quickest way to get all the pieces at once. Buying separately lets you pick a better filter, which is where kits usually skimp.

What has to grow with the tank

Moving to a bigger tank is not just more water. Three other things are sized to the water volume, so they change too.

The filter: two to three times the water volume

Turtles are far messier than fish. They eat in the water, defecate in the water, and shred things. The standard advice in the book is a filter rated for two to three times your actual water volume: a 20-gallon turtle tank wants a filter sold for 40 to 60 gallons. Canister filters are the usual recommendation once the tank gets big; for a small tank, a dedicated aquatic turtle filter that sits low in shallow water is fine.

Apply the same multiplier when you size up. Using the table above, a turtle with a 4-inch shell needs about 40 gallons of water, and that water wants a filter sold for roughly 80 to 120 gallons.

Water changes: 25 to 50 percent a week

Even with a good filter, you change water. A 25 to 50 percent change every week is normal for a small tank, with dechlorinator added to the new water and the new water matched to roughly the tank's temperature so the turtle does not get a cold shock. On a 20-gallon tank, that is 5 to 10 gallons a week.

Feeding in a separate container of water and tipping it out afterwards keeps a surprising amount of waste out of the main tank, which helps at any size.

The layout: one warm end, one cool end

A longer tank also makes the layout work better. The book puts heat and light over the dry dock at one end so the turtle can choose between warm-and-bright and cool-and-dim, which is how a turtle regulates its own temperature. The heater and filter go at the other end, where the filter's current spreads the heater's warmth. A tank with real length gives that gradient room to exist.

The water itself still has to stay in the book's "fine" band of 76 to 82 °F (about 24.5 to 28 °C), held by a submersible heater with its own thermostat. A bigger volume of water does not change that number; it only changes how much the heater has to warm.

Checklist

  • Measure the shell and plan on about 10 gallons of water per inch.
  • Assume growth: sliders grow fast, and an adult can need 75 gallons or more.
  • Note the date the turtle arrived and re-measure the shell now and then, so a too-small tank is caught early.
  • For a first tank, a clear storage tote works; pick one longer than it is tall.
  • Size the filter at two to three times the actual water volume, and resize it when the tank grows.
  • Change 25 to 50 percent of the water weekly, dechlorinated and temperature-matched.
  • Heat and light over the dock at one end, heater and filter at the other.
  • Keep the water at 76 to 82 °F with a thermostatic heater, whatever the tank size.
  • Check a care sheet for your species, and ask a reptile vet if anything looks off.

item.title: Owefolk: split shared expenses and settle up without the awkward part
item.description: Owefolk splits group expenses by shares, amounts or percentages, scans receipts on-device, translates into 50+ languages and only counts confirmed payments.
item.content:encoded:
Shared costs are easy to start and hard to finish. Someone covers dinner, someone else books the rental, a subscription gets split four ways, and a month later nobody is sure who owes what. Owefolk is built to keep that math clear, so the money question never turns into a friendship question.

What it does

  • Clear balances. After you sign in you see your net balance, what you owe, who owes you, and which group each number comes from, down to the cent.
  • Flexible splits. Split dinners, rent, trips and subscriptions by equal shares, exact amounts or custom percentages, and record who actually paid.
  • On-device receipt scanning. Point the camera at a receipt and the app reads the merchant and total.
  • On-device translation. Group names, expenses, balances and the activity feed in your language, chosen from 50+ languages.
  • One-tap settling. When someone owes you, the app shows the exact amount and jumps to Venmo, Cash App, PayPal, Zelle or a custom payment link.
  • Confirmed payments only. A payment counts only after the sender marks it sent and the recipient confirms it.
  • Shared history. Everyone in a group sees the same activity history.

Why "only real money moves count" matters

A common weak spot in shared-expense tracking is the gap between "will pay" and "has paid". Owefolk closes it with a two-step rule. Opening a payment app does not count as paying. You mark a payment as sent only after you have really sent it, and the balance changes only when the person receiving it confirms. Combined with the shared activity history, that means both sides always see the same story.

Choosing a split

Not every cost is split evenly, and Owefolk does not assume it is:

Split typeGood for
Equal sharesA group dinner where everyone ate about the same
Exact amountsA bill where each person's items are known
Custom percentagesRent or a shared plan where people pay different portions

Whatever you pick, the expense is tracked against the person who actually paid, so the balances stay honest.

What stays on your phone

Two features that usually rely on outside services run on the device here:

  • Receipt scanning uses on-device recognition, and the listing says your receipt photos never leave your phone.
  • Translation happens on the device too, so no text is sent to a translation service.

Diagnostics are anonymous and can be switched off, and you can delete your account at any time. Note that the app does use an account: you sign in to see balances and share groups.

Getting started

  1. Sign in and pick your language during onboarding (you can change it later in settings).
  2. Create a group for the trip, the apartment or the dinner club.
  3. Add expenses as they happen, choosing how each one is split.
  4. When it is time to settle, use the payment shortcuts, mark the payment sent once it really is, and let the other person confirm.

Good to know

  • Price: free to download.
  • Ads and purchases: the Google Play listing marks it as containing ads and offering in-app purchases.
  • Account: sign-in is required; account deletion is available any time.
  • Category and rating: Finance, rated Everyone.
  • Owefolk tracks who owes what. Money itself moves through the payment app you choose.

Is it for you?

  • You split costs with roommates, a partner, a trip group or friends.
  • You want splits by shares, exact amounts or percentages, not just "divide by four".
  • You want receipts scanned and text translated without sending them to an outside service.
  • You want balances to change only when a payment is actually confirmed.

item.title: The wrong server for the job
item.description: Using one program for everything wastes resources and hurts playback.
item.content:encoded:
Most people start a media server with a single program. They install Jellyfin and try to make it play music, audiobooks, and movies all at once. That is the trap. A media server is not a Swiss Army knife; it is a specialized tool for a specific job. When you force one program to handle every file type, you fight its design. The file organization becomes messy, the database gets bloated, and the app feels slow. The book calls this the "one program for everything" mistake. The result is a library that feels like a broken file browser instead of a polished streaming service.

The trap: one program for everything

The book warns that a media server does not find media for you. It only serves the files you give it. You cannot fix a bad folder layout by choosing a different program. However, you can choose the right program for the right media. The book explains that films, music, and audiobooks have different needs. Trying to satisfy all of them with one tool is a mistake.

Jellyfin is built for films and series. It needs artwork, episode order, subtitles, and several audio tracks. It also needs transcoding for phones and old TVs. Navidrome is built for music. It needs fast browsing by artist and album across tens of thousands of tracks, gapless playback, and good phone apps with offline caching. Audiobookshelf is built for audiobooks and podcasts. It needs chapter support, playback speed, bookmarks, and progress that syncs between devices.

If you put music in Jellyfin, you fight its interface. If you put audiobooks in Navidrome, you fight its layout. The book suggests a better approach. It recommends running three small servers. Each server reads its own part of the media share and keeps its own small database. This separation means each program does exactly what it is good at.

The fix: three servers, three media types

The book lays out a clear architecture. You do not need to buy new hardware. You can run all three as containers. They read from the same media share, so you do not duplicate files. The book states that Navidrome and Audiobookshelf are light. Only Jellyfin needs real resources when it transcodes. This saves money and keeps your system responsive.

The servers share the media folder. You organize your files by type. You put movies in one folder, music in another, and audiobooks in a third. The servers scan these folders separately. Jellyfin only looks at the movie folder. Navidrome only looks at the music folder. Audiobookshelf only looks at the audiobook folder. This keeps the databases small and the scans fast.

The book also notes that each server has its own config and database. These live on fast local storage, separate from the media. This follows the rule "Config and media apart." You can back up the database of one server without touching the media files. You can move the database to a different drive if you need to.

The fix: direct play first, GPU transcoding second

The book follows a specific rule for playback. It says "Direct play first, GPU transcoding second, CPU transcoding never by design." This means you should configure your servers to try direct play before converting the file. If the client cannot play the file, you use the GPU for transcoding. You should never use the CPU for transcoding.

This rule applies to all three servers. However, it is most important for Jellyfin. Jellyfin is the only server that needs real resources when it transcodes. Navidrome and Audiobookshelf are light. They do not need to transcode. They only need to stream the file to the client. The book emphasizes that you should keep the CPU free for other tasks.

The book covers this in Chapter 7. It shows how to get most playback to need no conversion at all. This reduces the load on the server. It also improves the quality of the stream. You get the full bitrate and the full quality of the file. The client app handles the rest.

The fix: private by default

The book also has a rule about security. It says "Private by default. Reach the servers from outside through your tailnet. A public URL is an exception you choose on purpose, with a reverse proxy and HTTPS in front." This means you should not expose your servers to the open internet. You should use a tailnet to reach them.

A tailnet is a private network. It connects your devices to your servers without exposing them to the public. You can use Tailscale or ZeroTier for this. The book recommends using a reverse proxy and HTTPS in front of the public URL. This adds an extra layer of security. It also encrypts the traffic.

The book warns that a media server on the open internet is a target like any other web app. Chapter 8 exists because of this. It shows how to make an exposed port safe. However, the book prefers to keep the servers private. You can still access them from outside your home network, but you do it through the tailnet.

Checklist

  • Run three separate servers for films, music, and audiobooks.
  • Put each media type in its own folder on the shared media share.
  • Configure Jellyfin to read only the film folder.
  • Configure Navidrome to read only the music folder.
  • Configure Audiobookshelf to read only the audiobook folder.

item.title: TipsyBuddy: track drinks, estimate BAC and get home safe
item.description: A night-out companion for Android that logs drinks, shows an estimated BAC and sober countdown, shares a live location link and puts rides one tap away.
item.content:encoded:
A night out goes better when you have a rough idea of where you stand: how many drinks, how much you have spent, and whether your friends know where you are. Counting in your head stops working after the second round. TipsyBuddy is a night-out companion that keeps that count for you, gives you an estimate of your blood alcohol content, and makes getting home safely a one-tap job.

One thing first, because the app itself puts it front and center: every number TipsyBuddy shows is an estimate for informational and harm-reduction purposes. It is not a breathalyzer, and it is never a reason to drive.

What it does

  • Quick drink logging. One-tap buttons for beer, wine, cocktails, shots and water, plus custom drinks with your own ABV, volume and cost.
  • Estimated BAC and sober countdown. A gauge based on your profile, color-coded zones (Sober, Buzzed, Tipsy, Elevated) and a timer showing roughly when you will feel back to baseline.
  • Running tab. A drink counter and a spending total, so the end-of-night bill is not a surprise.
  • Hydration nudges. Water reminders between alcoholic drinks, a next-day hangover risk score with recovery advice, and hydration tips before bed.
  • Live location sharing. Send friends a live map link that lasts from 30 minutes up to 4 hours.
  • Rides and emergency dialing. One-tap Uber or Lyft to your current location, speed dial for a trusted contact or local emergency services, and easy address copy for a designated driver.
  • History and trends. A monthly calendar of light, moderate, heavy and sober days, sober streaks and monthly spending.
  • Wear OS companion. BAC estimate, countdown and quick-add drinks on your watch.

How the estimate works

TipsyBuddy uses the Widmark formula, a standard physiological formula, with the profile you enter. The listing is clear about its limits: metabolism varies a lot with food, hydration, medications, fatigue and individual biology. Treat the gauge as a pacing aid, a reason to have a water or call it a night, not as a measurement.

Sharing your night

The live link is designed to be easy for the people you send it to. Friends open it in any browser, on any phone or PC, with no app download or sign-up. They can see your live location, your venue check-in and your phone's battery level. The link only works for whoever you send it to and expires on its own.

Privacy

According to the listing, your drinks, spending and health data stay on your device, and the monthly statistics are private on-device statistics. Location sharing is opt-in, reachable only through the unique link you share, and it expires automatically.

Good to know

  • Price: free to download, with ads.
  • Subscription: an optional ad-free subscription removes banners and interstitials. You manage or cancel it through Google Play subscriptions.
  • Rating: Mature 17+, in the Food & Drink category.
  • Safety notice from the app: estimates are for informational and harm-reduction purposes only. Never drink and drive. Always use a designated driver, taxi or rideshare. If you or someone near you needs urgent medical care, call your local emergency services immediately.

Is it for you?

  • You want a quick way to count drinks and see what the night is costing.
  • You like a gentle nudge to drink water between rounds.
  • You want friends to be able to follow you home on a live map without installing anything.
  • You understand the BAC number is an estimate and plan your ride home regardless.

item.content:encoded:

Reading the line

hour77 AM
day of month*every day
month*every month
day of week*every day of the week

So: minute 0 of hour 7, every day. "Scheduled caffeine" sits on the pill underneath, and the design is printed on both sides so it reads right in either hand.

item.title: Google Play's 12-tester rule: why your 14 days reset
item.description: New personal Google Play developer accounts must run a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days before production unlocks. Here is how the clock really counts, how to set the test up, and how to answer the production access application.
item.content:encoded:
You finished the app, built a signed bundle and opened Play Console, ready to ship. Then the Production page is locked. Ship Your First Android App gives this its own chapter, because it is the one step in publishing that comes with a calendar attached and no amount of coding speeds it up.

The rule, in Google's words

Google's "App testing requirements for new personal developer accounts" page states it plainly: developers with personal accounts created after November 13, 2023 must run a closed test for their app with a minimum of 12 testers who have been opted in continuously for at least 14 days. Until then, Production and features such as Pre-registration stay disabled in Play Console.

Organization accounts, and personal accounts created before November 13, 2023, are not subject to it.

The trap: two words that reset your clock

Most people read "12 testers, 14 days" and start counting from the day the test goes live. The words that matter are "continuously" and "preceding". At least 12 testers must be opted in when you apply, and they must have been opted in continuously for the preceding 14 days.

That has consequences:

  • A tester who joins on day 10 has not been opted in for 14 days on day 14.
  • A tester who opts out on day 9 and back in on day 11 breaks their own streak.
  • Most drop-outs happen because a tester tidied up their apps.

So recruiting exactly 12 people is the fastest way to restart the clock. The safe plan is to recruit more than 12, so a few drop-outs do not reset you. The book's timeline sends the opt-in link to 15 to 20 people and gets everyone in during the first day or two.

The four tracks

Google Play does not have one "upload" button. It has tracks, all under Test and release in Play Console:

  • Internal testing: up to 100 testers you list by email, for fast checks by a few trusted people. It can run before app setup is finished, and builds usually reach testers within seconds.
  • Closed testing: testers you choose, by email lists or Google Groups. It starts after app setup is complete and is required before production for new personal accounts.
  • Open testing: a public beta anyone can join on Google Play, available once you have production access.
  • Production: the real release, locked for new personal accounts until production access is approved.

A few facts from Google's "Set up an open, closed, or internal test" page save confusion later. The first test link can take several hours to become available after you publish a test for the first time. And internal testers cannot also be in your closed test: a user who opts in to the internal test is no longer eligible for a closed or open test until they opt out of it. If you plan to count yourself as one of the 12, opt out of the internal test before the closed test begins.

The fix: set it up so the clock only runs once

Step 1, an internal test for yourself. Go to Test and release, then Testing, then Internal testing. On the Testers tab, create an email list with your own Google account. Create a new release, upload app-release.aab, add short release notes, save, and roll it out. Open the opt-in link on your phone, accept, and install from the Play Store. It is the first time you get the exact APKs Google Play generates from your bundle, signed with the app signing key.

Step 2, the closed test.

  1. Finish the app setup tasks first; a closed test can only start after app setup is complete.
  2. Go to Test and release, then Testing, then Closed testing, and create or manage the closed track.
  3. On the Testers tab, choose an email list, or choose Google Groups and enter an address like yourgroupname@googlegroups.com.
  4. Create a release with your bundle (a new versionCode if it is a new build) and roll it out.
  5. Check the countries and regions the test is available in.
  6. Once the test is live, copy the opt-in link and send it with instructions.

A Google Group is easier than an email list here. You add people once, they join and leave through the group, and you never edit the tester list in Play Console again. Use a group only you can add members to, so the test stays closed.

Tell testers the rule. Google's page marks it as important: inform testers they need to stay opted in continuously for at least 14 days. The book's sample message says it in one line: uninstalling is fine, but don't leave the test, or Google stops counting you. Give them clear steps to try and a feedback channel besides Play's private feedback.

Use the 14 days, don't just wait them out

The test is not a waiting room. Google asks you to respond to feedback and fix bugs during the test, and the production application asks what you changed. Keep a simple log: date, what a tester reported, what you did. Shipping one or two updated builds to the closed track during the 14 days is normal, and each new build needs a higher versionCode.

Applying for production

When at least 12 testers have been opted in for the preceding 14 days, the Dashboard offers Apply for production. The application has three sections:

  • About your closed test: how easy recruiting was, whether testers used all features, whether usage matched real-world use, and a summary of the feedback.
  • About your app or game: the target audience, how the app provides value, and an estimated first-year install range (not shown publicly).
  • About your production readiness: what you changed based on the test and how you decided the app was ready.

Answer from your log, specifically. A bug a tester reported, the fix, and the version it shipped in is the kind of answer the questions are designed for; "testers liked it" gives the reviewer nothing to approve. And don't leave the form half-done: if you click Discard or leave a section without clicking Next (or Apply on the last one), your changes are not saved.

Google reviews the application and emails the account owner, usually within seven days, occasionally longer. If Google decides the app needs more testing, the reasons it gives include fewer than 12 opted-in testers or insufficient engagement. Review "is not a troubleshooting step": the app should already be stable, policy-compliant, rated correctly, and provide working login details under App access if it needs an account.

Checklist

  • [ ] Account verified, app created, setup tasks done
  • [ ] Internal test installed from Google Play on your own phone
  • [ ] You opted out of the internal test if you count as a closed tester
  • [ ] Closed test live with 15 to 20 people invited, all in during day one or two
  • [ ] Testers told: stay opted in for 14 straight days
  • [ ] A log of every report and fix, with builds using higher versionCodes
  • [ ] 12 or more testers opted in for the preceding 14 days before you apply
  • [ ] Every application section answered from the log, then Next or Apply clicked

item.title: Sticky Notes: Quick Widget, notes that live on your home screen
item.description: A lightweight Android app that puts colorful sticky notes on your home screen as widgets, with pinning, sharing and dark mode.
item.content:encoded:
Most note apps are good at storing things and bad at reminding you they exist. A note saved three screens deep is a note you never read again. Sticky Notes: Quick Widget takes the opposite approach: the note sits on your home screen, in your face, the way a paper sticky note sits on a monitor. You see it every time you unlock your phone.

What it does

  • Home screen widgets in multiple sizes, so a note can be a small square or a larger block.
  • Colors and styles. Pick a color per note, change the text size, choose a note style, or use a transparent background so it blends with your wallpaper.
  • Quick editing. Add a note in one tap and tap a widget to expand it.
  • Pin and dismiss. Pin the notes that matter and swipe away the ones you are done with.
  • Sharing. Send a note to someone else straight from the app.
  • Dark mode and a simple Material Design interface.

How to use it well

A home screen note works best when it stays short. A few patterns that suit this style of app:

  1. One note per job. A shopping list in one color, today's to-do items in another, so you can tell them apart at a glance.
  2. Pin the permanent ones. A door code, a phone number or an address you keep looking up can stay pinned, while short-lived notes get swiped away.
  3. Size by importance. Give the note you need most often a larger widget, and keep the rest small.
  4. Clear it when it is done. A note that has outlived its job becomes wallpaper. Swipe it away so the ones left on screen still mean something.

The listing suggests quick reminders, shopping lists, to-do items, phone numbers and addresses, and motivational quotes as typical uses.

Customizing the look

Because the notes live on your home screen, how they look matters more than in a normal app. You can change each note's color, adjust the text size so a list stays readable in a small widget, and pick a transparent background if you want the text to float over your wallpaper instead of sitting on a colored square. Dark mode is supported for the app itself.

Good to know

  • Price: free.
  • Ads: Google Play lists the app as containing ads.
  • In-app purchases: none are listed.
  • Size and battery: the listing describes a small app size and minimal battery usage.
  • Category and rating: Productivity, rated Everyone.
  • Devices: the listing says it works on all Android devices.

Is it for you?

  • You lose track of notes saved inside apps and want them on your home screen instead.
  • You keep a running shopping list or to-do list and want to see it every time you unlock.
  • You like to color-code things.

item.title: The infinite scroll trap
item.description: Putting a LazyColumn inside a vertically scrolling Column breaks layout. The book calls this the infinite scroll trap.
item.content:encoded:
The trap is thinking you can nest a scrolling list inside a scrolling container. The book warns that a lazy list composes only what is visible, but a vertically scrolling Column composes every child. When you put a LazyColumn inside a Column with Modifier.verticalScroll, the parent hands the lazy list infinite height. Compose throws an error. The book calls this the infinite scroll trap.

The trap: nesting scrolling containers

Compose lays out in a single pass. A parent hands each child constraints (a minimum and maximum width and height), the child picks a size inside them, and the parent places it. Modifiers like size, fillMaxWidth, padding and widthIn simply change the constraints on the way down. When a layout looks wrong, ask: what constraints did this child receive? That question solves most layout puzzles faster than trial and error. The book explains this flow in one paragraph. The trap is that a parent offering infinite height to a child that cannot fill it causes a crash. The book shows a code example of a Column with Modifier.verticalScroll. It then warns: WATCH OUT Never put a LazyColumn inside a vertically scrolling Column (Modifier.verticalScroll). The lazy list would be offered infinite height and Compose throws an error.

The fix: move headers and footers into the list

The book states that a lazy list composes only what is visible and reuses the slots as you scroll. It also says that two details make lists behave: Keys and animateItem(). The fix is to put headers and footers inside the lazy list with item { } instead of nesting them. The book provides a code example of a PantryList composable. It uses a LazyColumn with a modifier and contentPadding. Inside the LazyColumn, it uses an item block for a header Text. Then it uses items(items = items, key = { it.id }) to render the list. The book calls this the correct approach and warns against nesting.

The fix: use Scaffold for the screen frame

The book introduces Scaffold as the Material 3 layout for a full screen. It has slots for a top bar, a bottom bar, a floating action button and a snackbar host, and it calculates the padding your content needs so nothing hides behind them or behind the system bars. The book shows a code example of a PantryListScreen composable. It uses @OptIn(ExperimentalMaterial3Api::class) and @Composable. It builds a Scaffold with a topBar, a floatingActionButton, and an innerPadding lambda. Inside the innerPadding, it calls PantryList and passes the innerPadding as contentPadding. The book warns: COMMON MISTAKE Ignoring the innerPadding lambda parameter. Android Studio warns you, and for good reason: without it, your first list item sits under the top bar and the last one under the navigation bar. Pass it to the content, and for lists pass it as contentPadding so the list can still scroll behind the bars while its first and last items stay visible.

The fix: use Material components for rows

The book suggests that for rows, reach for Material's ListItem before building your own Row. It gives you correct spacing and typography, with slots for a headline, supporting text and leading or trailing content. The book calls this a list row for free. It shows a code example of a ListItem composable. It sets headlineContent, supportingContent, and trailingContent. It also applies a modifier for clickability. The book mentions other ready-made pieces worth knowing: Card and ElevatedCard, HorizontalDivider, LazyVerticalGrid(GridCells.Adaptive(160.dp)) for grids that adapt to width, PullToRefreshBox around a list, and ModalBottomSheet.

Checklist

  • Never put a LazyColumn inside a vertically scrolling Column
  • Use item { } for headers and footers inside the list
  • Use Scaffold for the screen frame
  • Pass innerPadding as contentPadding to the content
  • Use Material's ListItem for list rows

item.content:encoded:
A flashlight is the kind of tool you only think about when the power is out, the car keys are under the seat, or you are walking a dark driveway. At that moment you want light in one motion, not a hunt through menus. Flashlight: Torch + SOS is built around that idea: several fast ways to switch the light on, a screen light for softer situations, and an SOS mode for the moments that are more serious than a dropped key.

What it does

  • Camera flash torch. The main mode uses your phone's flash as a bright light source.
  • Screen light. Turns the display into a light panel with adjustable brightness and several colors, useful when a harsh flash is too much.
  • Stays on with the screen off. The torch keeps running after the display goes dark.
  • SOS mode. An emergency strobe and a Morse code SOS signal, with adjustable speed.
  • Shake to toggle. Shake the phone to switch the light on or off.
  • Quick settings tile, widget and notification controls. Start the light from the pull-down shade, from your home screen, or from the notification.
  • Auto-off timer. An optional timer switches the light off for you.
  • Themes and orientation. Light, dark and system themes, with portrait and landscape support.

Getting the light on fast

The useful thing about this app is the number of entry points. You do not have to open it at all most of the time:

  1. Add the quick settings tile to your pull-down shade. Swipe down, tap, light.
  2. Put the home screen widget next to the apps you use most, so the torch is one tap from unlocking.
  3. Turn on shake to toggle if you often need light with one hand busy.
  4. Use the notification controls to switch it off again without hunting for the app.

Pick whichever matches how you hold your phone in the dark. Many people end up using the tile for everyday use and the widget as a backup.

Screen light vs torch

The camera flash is the brightest option, but it is also narrow and harsh. The screen light is the gentler choice: reading a label, checking on someone sleeping, or lighting a small area close up. Because you can change both its color and brightness, you can dial it down until it is just enough. The listing notes that the screen light uses minimal power.

SOS mode

The SOS mode turns the light into a signal rather than a lamp. You get two styles:

  • an emergency strobe, a fast flashing light that draws attention, and
  • a Morse code SOS, the classic three short, three long, three short pattern.

The speed is adjustable. It is worth trying SOS mode once at home so you know where it is before you ever need it. A signal you can find in two seconds is far more useful than one you have to look for.

Battery

A torch that drains your phone defeats the purpose when you are already low. The listing describes the app as optimized for minimal battery drain, and the auto-off timer helps if you tend to forget the light is on in a pocket or bag.

Good to know

  • Price: free.
  • Ads: Google Play lists the app as containing ads.
  • In-app purchases: none are listed.
  • Category and rating: Tools, rated Everyone.
  • Devices: the listing says it works on all Android devices. The torch mode needs a phone with a camera flash; the screen light works on any screen.

Is it for you?

  • You want the torch on from the shade, a widget or a shake, without opening an app.
  • You want a softer, colored screen light as well as the bright flash.
  • You like having an SOS strobe and Morse signal ready on your phone.
  • You forget to turn lights off and would use an auto-off timer.

item.title: Leaving Google Photos for Immich: keep your dates, keep backups running, share with family
item.description: The move from Google Photos to Immich goes wrong in four quiet places. Takeout imports that land ten years of photos on today's date, phone backups that stall, one shared family login, and a reverse proxy that chokes on big videos. Here is the fix for each, plus a checklist.
item.content:encoded:
Getting Immich running is the easy part. The library is up, the timeline looks like Google Photos, and the first test photo shows up from your phone. The move itself is where it quietly goes wrong, and none of these problems throw an error. Ten years of photos land on today's date. The phone stops backing up and nobody notices for a month. The whole family shares one login, so face recognition and memories turn into a mess. A long video from your phone fails to upload through the proxy for no obvious reason.

This post walks through the migration in order. It assumes Immich is already installed the documented way, with the library on the data disk and the database on local SSD.

Before the first upload: storage template and a normal account

Two settings have to happen before anything goes in, because they are painful to change later.

The storage template. By default Immich stores files in folders named by internal IDs. Go to Administration → Settings → Storage Template and turn it on with a pattern like year/month/day. Your library on disk becomes a readable folder tree, which matters a lot the day you want to browse it without Immich or move to something else.

A normal account. The first user you create is the administrator. Use a strong, unique password for it, save it somewhere safe, and then create a separate, normal account for daily use. The phone app logs in with the normal account, never the admin one.

Trap 1: uploading the raw Takeout files

Google Takeout exports Google Photos as the original files plus JSON sidecar files. Those sidecars hold the dates and descriptions Google stripped from the photos themselves. If you unzip the archives and upload the raw files directly, the dates are lost and a decade of photos gets dumped onto today's date.

The fix: use a tool that reads the sidecars. A community tool called immich-go reads Takeout archives, matches each photo to its sidecar, and uploads everything with the right dates. Read its README and do a test run with one archive first. Check that a handful of old photos land on the right day in the timeline before you feed it the rest.

Then the order of the exit matters:

  1. Import everything and compare counts between Google Photos and Immich.
  2. Run one full backup of your Immich library (on Proxmox, that means the Docker VM on your backup server, plus the off-site copy).
  3. Only then delete anything from Google.
  4. Cancel the subscription last.

Trap 2: a phone backup that silently stalls

The phone app is what replaces Google's automatic backup, and it only works if the phone lets it run. Install the Immich app from the App Store or Google Play, enter your server URL, log in with your normal account, and then:

  1. Open the backup settings and choose which albums to back up. "Recents" or "Camera" covers most phones.
  2. Turn on background backup.
  3. On Android, exclude the app from battery optimization in the system settings. On iPhone, leave Background App Refresh on for Immich.
  4. Leave the app open on Wi-Fi for the first big upload. Background uploads are throttled by the phone and will take days for a 50 GB library.

Even set up right, background backup on phones is best effort, because the operating system decides when apps may run. The habit that catches a stall: open the app once a week and glance at the backup count. It takes two seconds and it is the only way you'll notice.

There is a second, slower way backups stop: the version. Immich moved to v3 in July 2026, and the server only talks to mobile apps of a compatible major version. Pin the server in .env so a major upgrade never happens by surprise:

IMMICH_VERSION=v3

When you do update, update the phone apps first, then the server.

Trap 3: one login for the whole family

Sharing one account feels simpler, and it breaks the parts of Immich people actually like. Every phone backs up into the same library, and face recognition and memories mix everyone together.

The fix: give every person their own Immich account, so each phone backs up into its owner's library. Then use the two sharing tools Immich gives you:

  • Partner sharing, in each user's account settings, lets a spouse see your whole timeline, and optionally show it mixed into their own. This is the "our photos" feeling people miss from Google.
  • Shared albums work like Google's: add people by their Immich account, and everyone can add photos. For relatives without an account, a shared link works too, but only if that link is reachable from the internet. That is an exposure decision, not a default.

If the data disk is small, set a storage quota per user under Administration → Users. One 4K video habit can fill a terabyte faster than you'd expect.

Trap 4: the proxy that drops big videos

Photos upload fine through a reverse proxy; long phone videos are what fail. Behind Nginx Proxy Manager, two settings save hours of confusion. Turn on Websockets Support on the proxy host, and add this to the host's Advanced tab so large videos upload:

client_max_body_size 50000M;
proxy_request_buffering off;
proxy_read_timeout 600s;
proxy_send_timeout 600s;
send_timeout 600s;

One more rule from the Immich docs: Immich must be served at the root of its own subdomain, like photos.example.com, not under a path like example.com/photos. Putting it under a path fails in confusing ways.

Checklist

  • Storage template (year/month/day) switched on before the first upload
  • A normal account for daily use, separate from the admin
  • Takeout imported with immich-go after a one-archive test run, sidecar dates intact
  • Counts match, and one full backup of Immich done, before anything is deleted from Google
  • Phone background backup on; battery optimization off (Android) or Background App Refresh on (iPhone)
  • First big upload done with the app open on Wi-Fi
  • Backup count glanced at once a week
  • IMMICH_VERSION=v3 pinned; phone apps updated before the server
  • One Immich account per person; partner sharing and shared albums instead of a shared login
  • Per-user storage quotas if the disk is small
  • Websockets on and the large-upload settings in the proxy's Advanced tab
  • Immich on its own subdomain, never under a path

item.title: NUT shutdown on a timer: upssched, secondaries first, and HOSTSYNC explained
item.description: Network UPS Tools can shut your homelab down after N minutes on battery instead of waiting for "low battery". How a NUT shutdown runs, a Debian secondary client, TrueNAS as a client, an upssched timer with its script and tmpfiles rule, and the timing settings that matter.
item.content:encoded:
A NUT server that shuts itself down perfectly is not enough. If the NAS was never told, or the Docker host in the corner was never told, the outage still ends in a crash. And by default NUT waits for the UPS to report low battery, a threshold the UPS picks and an estimate that gets optimistic as the battery ages. This post connects the clients, explains the order NUT shuts things down in, and replaces "wait for low battery" with a timed shutdown that keeps most of the battery in reserve.

The examples assume the UPS's USB cable is on a Proxmox host running the NUT server (upsd) and the primary upsmon, with the UPS named myups at 10.0.10.5.

How a NUT shutdown actually runs

When the UPS goes critical (on battery and low battery, or the forced-shutdown flag is set), this is the sequence:

  1. The primary upsmon notices and sets the FSD (forced shutdown) flag on the UPS in upsd.
  2. Every secondary upsmon sees FSD on its next poll, waits FINALDELAY seconds and runs its own SHUTDOWNCMD. As it shuts down, it disconnects from upsd.
  3. The primary waits until all secondaries have disconnected, or until HOSTSYNC seconds have passed, whichever comes first.
  4. The primary shuts its own machine down, creating the POWERDOWNFLAG file on the way.
  5. Late in the primary's shutdown, that flag tells the driver to command the UPS to cut its output after offdelay seconds.

That ordering is built in: secondaries always go before the primary. Put the NAS, the other servers and any VMs that run elsewhere on secondaries, and keep the primary on the machine with the UPS cable.

A Debian client

On another Debian or Ubuntu machine that should shut down with the UPS, install only the client part:

apt install nut-client

Set the mode in /etc/nut/nut.conf:

MODE=netclient

Then point upsmon at the server with a secondary user you created in upsd.users:

# /etc/nut/upsmon.conf
MONITOR myups@10.0.10.5 1 upsmon_remote CHANGE-ME-long-random secondary

MINSUPPLIES 1
SHUTDOWNCMD "/sbin/shutdown -h +0"
NOTIFYFLAG ONBATT   SYSLOG+WALL
NOTIFYFLAG ONLINE   SYSLOG+WALL
NOTIFYFLAG FSD      SYSLOG+WALL
NOTIFYFLAG COMMBAD  SYSLOG+WALL

Lock the file down, start the monitor and check that the client can read the UPS:

chown root:nut /etc/nut/upsmon.conf
chmod 0640 /etc/nut/upsmon.conf
systemctl enable --now nut-monitor.service
upsc myups@10.0.10.5 ups.status

A secondary never has a POWERDOWNFLAG: only the primary tells the UPS to cut power. Treat the secondary password as a low-value credential that only lets a client follow the UPS, and never reuse the admin password on a client.

TrueNAS as a client

TrueNAS has a built-in UPS service that is NUT underneath. In TrueNAS 25.10 it is under System > Services > UPS (the pencil icon). Set Identifier to myups, UPS Mode to Slave (TrueNAS still uses the old word for a secondary), Remote Hostname and Remote Port to the server and 3493, and the monitor user and password. Save, turn the service on and set it to start automatically. Menu names have moved between TrueNAS releases, so check the UPS service page in the docs for your version if the screen looks different.

The NAS is usually the machine whose clean shutdown matters most and takes longest. Time it. By default a secondary upsmon logs off upsd as soon as it has started its shutdown, so HOSTSYNC only covers that hand-off, not the whole NAS shutdown. What protects the rest of it is the time the primary's own shutdown takes plus the UPS's offdelay; make sure those together are longer than the NAS needs.

Shutdown on a timer, not on low battery

The alternative to the UPS's low-battery threshold is to decide for yourself: if the UPS has been on battery for N minutes, the outage is real, so shut everything down while the battery is still mostly full. NUT does this with upssched, a timer helper that upsmon calls on events.

On the primary, tell upsmon to call upssched for the on-battery and on-line events:

# add to /etc/nut/upsmon.conf on the primary
NOTIFYCMD /sbin/upssched
NOTIFYFLAG ONBATT SYSLOG+WALL+EXEC
NOTIFYFLAG ONLINE SYSLOG+WALL+EXEC

Check the real path with command -v upssched and use that. Then configure the timer. The stock upssched.conf ships with PIPEFN disabled on purpose, so you set it deliberately:

# /etc/nut/upssched.conf
CMDSCRIPT /etc/nut/upssched-cmd
PIPEFN /run/nut/upssched/upssched.pipe
LOCKFN /run/nut/upssched/upssched.lock

AT ONBATT * START-TIMER onbatt 180
AT ONLINE * CANCEL-TIMER onbatt

START-TIMER onbatt 180 starts a three-minute timer when the UPS goes on battery, and CANCEL-TIMER stops it if power comes back first. If the timer runs out, upssched runs CMDSCRIPT with the timer name as its argument. Pick the number from your own runtime at your real load, not from the box.

The script:

#!/bin/sh
# /etc/nut/upssched-cmd
case "$1" in
  onbatt)
    logger -t upssched-cmd "On battery for too long, forcing shutdown"
    /sbin/upsmon -c fsd
    ;;
  *)
    logger -t upssched-cmd "Unrecognized timer: $1"
    ;;
esac

upsmon -c fsd sets the forced-shutdown flag from the primary, which starts the normal ordered shutdown: secondaries first, then the primary. Create the directory for the pipe and lock file, owned by the user upsmon runs as (nut on Debian), make the script executable, and restart:

install -d -o nut -g nut -m 0750 /run/nut/upssched
chmod 0750 /etc/nut/upssched-cmd
chown root:nut /etc/nut/upssched-cmd /etc/nut/upssched.conf
systemctl restart nut-monitor.service

/run is cleared at every boot, so the directory has to be recreated each time. A one-line tmpfiles rule does it:

# /etc/tmpfiles.d/nut-upssched.conf
d /run/nut/upssched 0750 nut nut -

Do not test the timer by pulling the plug before the script works. Run the script by hand first, with a short timer, at a time when a real shutdown costs nothing.

The timing settings

SettingWhereDefaultChange it when
HOSTSYNCPrimary upsmon.conf15 sYour slowest secondary needs longer to disconnect
FINALDELAYEvery upsmon.conf5 sYou want more warning before SHUTDOWNCMD; keep it below the primary's HOSTSYNC
DEADTIMEEvery upsmon.conf15 sRarely; keep it a multiple of POLLFREQ
POLLFREQEvery upsmon.conf5 sRarely
START-TIMERPrimary upssched.confnoneYour own choice from your measured runtime

Home Assistant, for eyes only

Home Assistant's Network UPS Tools integration does not shut anything down; it reads the NUT server so you can see the UPS on a dashboard and get a phone notification when it goes on battery. Give it its own user with no upsmon, actions or instcmds lines in upsd.users, so it can read status but change nothing, and reload upsd with systemctl reload nut-server.

Checklist

  • Every machine that needs a clean shutdown runs a secondary upsmon or its own UPS client.
  • upsc myups@<server> works from each client.
  • TrueNAS's UPS service is a secondary pointed at the server, enabled at boot.
  • The primary's shutdown time plus offdelay is longer than the NAS needs.
  • The upssched timer, script and tmpfiles rule are in place, and the script was tested by hand.

item.title: Troubleshooting a Linux server in a fixed order: running, listening, reachable, logs, changes
item.description: A boring, repeatable order for fixing a broken Linux service, with the one command that answers each question. Plus load average read honestly, memory by the available column, OOM kills, a full disk, and a symptom-to-first-command table.
item.content:encoded:
Something on the server is broken, and the instinct is to start changing things: restart the service, then the VM, then edit a config you half remember, then reinstall a package. Sometimes it comes back and you never learn why. Often you have now changed four things and broken a fifth. Good troubleshooting is boring on purpose: a fixed order of questions, each answered by a command, and no changes until you know what is wrong.

The fixed order

Stop at the first unexpected answer and work there.

  1. Is it running? systemctl status app, or docker ps for containers.
  2. Is it listening? sudo ss -tulpn | grep 8080 shows the port and the address it is bound to.
  3. Can you reach it? From the server: curl -v http://127.0.0.1:8080/. From your laptop: the same with the server's address. The difference between those two answers is a bind address, a firewall or the network.
  4. What do the logs say? journalctl -u app -n 100, then journalctl -p err -b for everything else that went wrong this boot.
  5. What changed? Most outages follow a change. Find it:
tail -n 30 /var/log/apt/history.log             # recent package changes
sudo find /etc -mtime -2 -type f 2>/dev/null    # config changed in 2 days
journalctl --list-boots | tail -3               # did it reboot?
journalctl -b -1 -n 20 --no-pager               # end of the previous boot
uptime

On Debian 13 the last command is gone; the previous boot's journal answers the same question.

The rule that makes the whole order work: write down every change you make while troubleshooting, with the time. A text file in your home directory is enough. If the fix does not work, you can undo exactly what you did. And before changing anything on a VM you care about, take a snapshot, so a bad "fix" is two seconds from undone.

Is the machine itself healthy?

When the problem is "everything is slow" rather than "one thing is broken", look at the whole machine:

uptime          # how long it has run, and the load averages
top             # live: CPU, memory, processes (q to quit)
free -h         # memory and swap
df -h           # disk space per filesystem
sudo iotop -o   # who is using the disk right now (sudo apt install iotop)

Load average, honestly

$ uptime
 10:42:17 up 12 days,  3:05,  2 users,  load average: 3.84, 2.10, 0.95

The three numbers are the average number of processes that were running or waiting to run over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. On Linux, processes waiting for disk I/O count too. Read them against the number of cores (nproc): on a 4-core VM, a load around 4 means the CPUs are fully busy, and well above it means work is queueing. The trend matters as much as the value: 3.84, 2.10, 0.95 is climbing, so something started recently. A high load with idle CPUs in top (low us and sy, high wa) points at the disk, not the processor.

Memory and swap

$ free -h
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:           3.8Gi       2.9Gi       121Mi        12Mi       1.0Gi       880Mi
Swap:          975Mi       410Mi       565Mi

A small free value is not a problem: Linux uses spare memory as disk cache and gives it back when programs need it. The column that matters is available. Swap in use is not a problem by itself; swap that keeps growing while available stays low means the machine needs more memory or a process is leaking. In top, press M to sort by memory.

When the kernel kills something

When memory runs out completely, the kernel's out-of-memory killer picks a process and kills it. The service just "dies", sometimes restarted by systemd, and its own log says nothing useful. The kernel log does:

journalctl -k -b | grep -i -E 'out of memory|oom'
sudo dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'killed process|oom'

The fix is never "turn off the OOM killer". Give the VM more memory, cap the hungry service (MemoryMax= in a systemd drop-in, or a memory limit on the container), or move it somewhere with room.

Disk full

A full root filesystem breaks things in strange ways: services fail to start, logins hang, APT cannot write its lists, databases go read-only. Find where the space went, from the top down:

df -h                                          # which filesystem is full?
df -i                                          # or out of inodes?
sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h | tail   # which top-level directory?
sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h | tail
sudo find / -xdev -type f -size +500M -exec ls -lh {} + 2>/dev/null

The usual suspects:

WhereWhat fills itFix
/var/log/journalThe journal with no size capjournalctl --vacuum-size=200M, then cap it
/var/cache/aptDownloaded package filessudo apt clean
/var/lib/dockerOld images, stopped containers, build cachedocker system df, then prune carefully
/var/log/*.logAn app logging in a loopFix the loop, then truncate the file
Deleted but openA deleted file a process still writes tosudo lsof +L1, restart that process

Do not delete a log file that a running service is still writing to: the space is not freed until the service closes it. Truncate it instead with sudo truncate -s 0 /var/log/app.log. And never delete files in /var/lib/docker by hand; use Docker's own prune commands.

Symptom to first command

Where to start looking for the most common complaints. It is a starting point, not a diagnosis.

SymptomFirst commandLook for
Service will not startjournalctl -u app -n 50The first real error line
Works locally, not from LANsudo ss -tulpnBound to 127.0.0.1, or a firewall
"Connection refused"sudo ss -tlpn 'sport = :PORT'Nothing listening on that port
Timeout connectingsudo nft list rulesetA drop rule, here or on the router
Name does not resolvedig name and dig @router nameWhich DNS server is wrong
Service dies randomlyjournalctl -k -b with grep oomThe OOM killer
Cannot write filesdf -h and df -iA full filesystem or no inodes
"Permission denied"namei -l /pathThe missing permission on the path
Broke after an updatetail /var/log/apt/history.logWhat changed, and when
SSH refusedsudo sshd -t from the consoleA config error after an edit

Asking for help well

When the answer is in a forum or a bug tracker, the people there can only help with what you show them:

  • The exact command you ran and its exact output, copied, not paraphrased.
  • The relevant log lines (journalctl -u app -n 50 --no-pager), with secrets removed.
  • Versions: cat /etc/debian_version, uname -r, and the app's version.
  • What you already tried, and what changed before it broke.

Writing that down often solves the problem before you post it, and it is exactly the note you will want next time.

Checklist

  • Follow the order: running, listening, reachable, logs, changes.
  • Write down every change you make while troubleshooting.
  • Snapshot before trying a fix on anything important.
  • Read load average against nproc, and memory by the available column.
  • Check the kernel log for OOM kills when a service dies without a reason.
  • Truncate live logs instead of deleting them.

item.title: Frigate recording retention: continuous, motion and alerts, and how big a disk you need
item.description: Frigate keeps continuous, motion and alert/detection footage on separate clocks. The three retention plans from the Frigate docs, the storage arithmetic for your bitrates, what happens when the disk fills anyway, and what to back up.
item.content:encoded:
Recording is the easy part of a Frigate NVR to switch on and the hard part to size. Without a plan, one of two things happens. Either retention is set to "30 days of everything" and the disk fills in a week, at which point Frigate starts deleting the oldest footage on its own; or retention is so short that the clip you needed from last Tuesday is already gone. A retention plan is a short calculation and a few numbers in config.yml. This post walks through both.

What Frigate keeps

Frigate records in short segments and keeps three kinds of footage, each with its own retention:

  • Continuous: all video, whether or not anything moved.
  • Motion: only segments in which motion was detected.
  • Alerts and detections: segments that overlap a review item, with a few seconds before and after (pre_capture and post_capture, both 5 seconds by default).

Each kind has its own number of days. A segment that overlaps an alert is the one you most want to keep, so give alerts the most days. Retention for alerts and detections also has a mode:

ModeWhat is kept for the review item's retention
allEvery segment that overlaps the review item
motionOnly overlapping segments with motion
active_objectsOnly overlapping segments with an active (moving) tracked object

Three plans from the documentation

Frigate's recording documentation gives three starting points. Pick the one that matches what you would need after an incident.

Keep everything for a while. All video for 3 days, motion for 7 days, and anything overlapping an alert or detection for 30 days:

record:
  enabled: true
  continuous:
    days: 3
  motion:
    days: 7
  alerts:
    retain:
      days: 30
      mode: all
  detections:
    retain:
      days: 30
      mode: all

Reduced storage. No continuous retention; motion for 3 days; alerts and detections for 30 days, keeping only their segments with motion:

record:
  enabled: true
  motion:
    days: 3
  alerts:
    retain:
      days: 30
      mode: motion
  detections:
    retain:
      days: 30
      mode: motion

Alerts only. Video is discarded unless an alert is ongoing; alerts are kept for 30 days:

record:
  enabled: true
  continuous:
    days: 0
  alerts:
    retain:
      days: 30
      mode: motion

Continuous footage is what answers "what happened in the driveway at 3 a.m." when nothing was detected, which is why the first plan is a good default if the disk allows it. Retention values can be set globally, as above, and overridden per camera. Days may be decimals, so 0.5 keeps twelve hours.

Storage arithmetic

The disk you need depends on the bitrate of each camera's main stream and the plan you picked. The upper bound is continuous recording:

GB per day per camera = bitrate (Mbit/s) x 86,400 / 8 / 1,000

  2 Mbit/s  ->  21.6 GB/day
  4 Mbit/s  ->  43.2 GB/day
  6 Mbit/s  ->  64.8 GB/day
  8 Mbit/s  ->  86.4 GB/day

For the first plan, estimate each layer separately and add them. Continuous days are the full rate. Motion days and alert days are a fraction of it, and that fraction depends entirely on the scene: a camera on a quiet back garden may see motion a small part of the day, one facing a street much more. A worked example, arithmetic only:

4 cameras at 4 Mbit/s

Continuous, 3 days:      4 x 43.2 GB x 3          = 518 GB
Motion days 4-7:         4 x 43.2 GB x 4 x 0.20   = 138 GB   (assume 20% motion)
Alerts/detections 8-30:  4 x 43.2 GB x 23 x 0.05  = 199 GB   (assume 5% activity)
                                           Total  ~ 855 GB  -> plan for a 2 TB disk

The 20 and 5 percent figures are assumptions to replace with your own. After a few days, open System > Storage in Frigate: it shows how much space each camera's recordings use, which gives you a real per-day figure. That page counts Frigate's recordings only; for the disk itself, use df -h on the host.

Leave at least 20 percent of the disk free in the plan. Bitrates rise at night and in rain, cameras get added, and the emergency cleanup below works from the disk's real free space.

When the disk fills anyway

Frigate watches the free space of the disk holding /media/frigate/recordings. When less than roughly one hour of recording space remains, estimated from the current bitrate, it deletes the oldest recordings first, regardless of your retention settings, and logs a message. Two consequences follow:

  • Anything else filling that disk, even files that are not Frigate's, can trigger deletion of your oldest recordings. Keep the recordings disk for recordings only.
  • Frequent emergency cleanups mean your retention is larger than the disk. Reduce the days until normal retention keeps up.

Also check from inside the container that /media/frigate really is the disk you think it is:

docker exec frigate df -h /media/frigate

If a disk or NFS share is not actually mounted there, Frigate fills whatever filesystem is underneath, usually the system disk. If you record to a NAS, a dedicated dataset with its own quota keeps a runaway Frigate from filling the rest of the NAS, and keeps the NAS's other files from triggering Frigate's cleanup.

Snapshots and exports

Snapshots are still images of tracked objects. They are what Home Assistant attaches to notifications, and they are off by default. Turn them on and give them their own retention:

snapshots:
  enabled: true
  bounding_box: true
  retain:
    default: 30

Exports are how you keep a specific clip beyond retention. Use the Export button in the History view (or right-click a review item), choose the time range and give it a name. Exports are saved separately and are not removed by retention. Download an export to hand a clip to someone instead of copying files out of the recordings folder.

H.265 recordings on Apple devices

If a camera records an H.265 main stream, Safari on macOS and iPhone may refuse to play its recordings. Frigate has a per-camera setting for this:

cameras:
  driveway:
    ffmpeg:
      apple_compatibility: true

Test playback from every device that will view recordings, including the Home Assistant app, before you rely on it.

What to back up

The recordings themselves are rarely backed up: they are large, they expire by design, and the important clips are exports. What you must back up is small:

  • config.yml (your whole configuration)
  • frigate.db (review items, tracked objects, users), copied while Frigate is stopped or with SQLite's backup command
  • your compose.yaml and .env
  • the exports you want to keep, copied off the Frigate disk

If Frigate runs in a Proxmox VM, a VM backup covers all of it. Untick Backup on the recordings disk in the VM's Hardware tab so the backup skips the footage.

Checklist

  • Plan chosen and written down: continuous, motion and alert/detection days.
  • Storage estimate done with your real bitrates, plus 20 percent headroom.
  • The record block in config.yml matches the plan.
  • Snapshots enabled with retention.
  • The recordings disk holds nothing but Frigate media.
  • docker exec frigate df -h /media/frigate shows the right disk.
  • Storage page checked after a week, retention adjusted.
  • Config, database and compose files are in your backups.

item.title: Your cast button went grey after the IoT VLAN: fix discovery without tearing down the wall
item.description: Moving smart devices to their own network usually breaks casting, AirPlay and printer discovery, and the tempting fix is a rule that lets IoT reach everything again. Here is why discovery breaks, the mDNS repeater and SSDP relay on OPNsense, when to give Home Assistant a second network card, and the NTP redirect for devices that ignore DHCP.
item.content:encoded:
The moment IoT moves to its own network, something stops working. The TV no longer shows up as a cast target, the speaker disappears from the AirPlay list, and the printer goes missing. Usually it is not the firewall rules. It is discovery: the way your phone finds the TV, the speaker or the printer by shouting on the local network and waiting for an answer. Those shouts do not cross a router.

The trap: one rule that undoes the whole point

The tempting fix is a rule that lets IoT reach everything again. It works, and it throws away the separation you just built. The right fix is to understand what the device is actually doing and pass exactly that.

Why discovery breaks

Most home discovery protocols use multicast, which is local to one network by design:

ProtocolAddress and portUsed by
mDNS (Bonjour)224.0.0.251, UDP 5353AirPlay, Chromecast, HomeKit, printers, ESPHome
SSDP (UPnP discovery)239.255.255.250, UDP 1900Smart TVs, Sonos, DLNA media servers, some consoles

A router does not forward multicast between subnets. Your phone on TRUSTED asks "is there a TV here?", the TV on IOT never hears it, and the cast button stays grey. Nothing is blocked; the question just never arrives.

It helps to keep the one rule behind every rule in mind: a zone may start connections to zones below it, never to zones above it, and replies are always allowed back because OPNsense is a stateful firewall. Your phone (trusted) casting to the TV (IoT) is downhill, so the trusted rules already allow the connection itself. Only the discovery question is missing.

Fix 1: an mDNS repeater

OPNsense has a plugin for this: os-mdns-repeater.

  1. System → Firmware → Plugins: install os-mdns-repeater.
  2. Services → mDNS Repeater: enable it and select the two interfaces it should bridge, TRUSTED and IOT.
  3. Do not add GUEST or MGMT.

The repeater only carries discovery. Once your phone knows the TV's address, it opens a normal connection to it, which your trusted rules already allow.

What the repeater does not do: it does not open any firewall ports, and it does not let IoT devices start connections into trusted. It copies small discovery packets between two networks. Your rules still decide everything else.

When casting finds the device but won't play

Some devices also need to connect back. Chromecast and AirPlay, for example, can open connections from the device to the phone during a session. If casting finds the device but fails to play:

  1. Open Firewall → Log Files → Live View and filter on that device's address.
  2. Look for blocked traffic from the device to the phone.
  3. Add one narrow pass rule on IOT: that device to TRUSTED net, with the ports you saw.

One device per rule. Not IOT net to everything.

Fix 2: SSDP with a broadcast relay

For SSDP devices, the os-udpbroadcastrelay plugin plays the same role. Configure an instance for:

  • UDP port 1900
  • multicast address 239.255.255.250
  • interfaces TRUSTED and IOT only

Like the mDNS repeater, give it only the interfaces that need it, and expect to add a narrow rule if a device needs to call back.

Fix 3: give Home Assistant a leg on IoT

Home Assistant uses discovery heavily: it finds ESPHome devices, Chromecasts, HomeKit accessories and many others by listening for multicast. You can make all of it work through repeaters, but there is a simpler option for Home Assistant specifically: add a second network card to its VM, tagged VLAN 30, so it sits directly on the IoT network as well as on servers.

That gives Home Assistant first-hand discovery with no repeater and no rule exceptions. The trade-off is real: Home Assistant now bridges two zones, so it has to be the best-patched machine in the house, with its own updates on and its admin accounts on strong passwords and two-factor login.

To choose, start with the question "who needs to discover the device?" Most homes end up with the repeater for phones and casting, and Home Assistant either on a second network card or reached through narrow rules.

Device by device

  • ESPHome devices report to Home Assistant over its API, and Home Assistant starts the connection, so ordinary downhill rules already cover it. Only discovery needs the repeater or the second network card.
  • MQTT devices (Zigbee2MQTT bridges, Tasmota, Shelly in MQTT mode) start the connection to the broker. If the broker is on servers, add one IOT rule: IOT net to the broker's address on port 1883 (or 8883 with TLS). That is an uphill exception, so keep it to the one host and port.
  • Printers need mDNS for discovery and IPP (TCP 631) from trusted, which is downhill and already allowed.
  • Cameras that record to a server on your own network: the recorder starts the connection to the camera (downhill), so no exception is needed. If they do not need the cloud, put their addresses in an alias such as IOT_LOCAL_ONLY and block that alias from the internet.

Time and DNS for devices that ignore DHCP

Some devices hardcode a public DNS server or time server and ignore what DHCP tells them. You can quietly redirect them to the firewall with a port forward on the IOT interface, under Firewall → NAT → Port Forward:

Interface:     IOT
Protocol:      UDP
Source:        IOT net
Destination:   ! IOT address   (anything except the firewall)
Port:          123 (NTP)
Redirect to:   127.0.0.1, port 123
Description:   Force IoT time to the firewall

Make sure the firewall's NTP service (Services → Network Time) listens on the IOT interface. The same redirect works for DNS on port 53. It cannot catch encrypted DNS (DNS over HTTPS on 443 or DNS over TLS on 853), which needs blocking separately.

Checklist: IoT that still works

  • [ ] mDNS repeater on TRUSTED and IOT only
  • [ ] SSDP relay only if a device needs it
  • [ ] Narrow pass rules for call-backs you saw in Live View, one device each
  • [ ] Home Assistant on a second network card in VLAN 30, or narrow rules instead
  • [ ] MQTT exception: IOT net to the broker host and port only
  • [ ] NTP (and DNS) redirected to the firewall on IOT
  • [ ] Local-only devices listed in IOT_LOCAL_ONLY and blocked from the internet

The wall between IoT and the rest of the house stays up. You just let the right questions through it.
