item.title: Gradle convention plugins for a multi-module Android app: build-logic, AGP 9 and the version catalog
item.description: Stop repeating twenty lines in every build.gradle.kts. How to set up a build-logic included build, write class-based convention plugins (library, Compose, Hilt, feature), keep compileSdk and minSdk in one place with AGP 9's CommonExtension, and use libs.versions.toml properly.
item.content:encoded:
Once an Android app has a dozen or more modules, every build.gradle.kts starts to repeat the same twenty lines: the Android plugin, compileSdk, minSdk, Java and Kotlin options, the Compose setup, the Hilt plugin and processor, the test dependencies. Bumping minSdk means editing every file, and forgetting one means a module that quietly builds differently from the rest.

Convention plugins fix that. A convention plugin is a small Gradle plugin you write yourself, which applies and configures other plugins the way your project wants. Each module then says what kind of module it is, a library or a feature, and the plugin supplies the how. Google's Now in Android sample is built this way, and Gradle's documentation recommends this approach over cross-project configuration with subprojects {} and allprojects {}.

buildSrc or build-logic

Gradle offers two places for shared build logic.

  • buildSrc is a special directory Gradle builds automatically before your project. It works, but any change inside it invalidates the whole build's configuration, because it is on the classpath of every build script.
  • An included build, by convention named build-logic, is a separate Gradle build that your main build includes with includeBuild. Its plugins are resolved by ID like any other plugin, and only the modules that apply a changed plugin are affected.

This post uses build-logic, as Now in Android does.

Setting up build-logic

MyApp/
├── build-logic/
│   ├── settings.gradle.kts
│   └── convention/
│       ├── build.gradle.kts
│       └── src/main/kotlin/
│           ├── AndroidLibraryConventionPlugin.kt
│           ├── AndroidLibraryComposeConventionPlugin.kt
│           ├── AndroidFeatureConventionPlugin.kt
│           ├── HiltConventionPlugin.kt
│           └── com/example/buildlogic/KotlinAndroid.kt
├── gradle/libs.versions.toml
└── settings.gradle.kts      // pluginManagement { includeBuild("build-logic") }

build-logic/settings.gradle.kts shares the main project's version catalog, so plugins and libraries have one source of versions:

// build-logic/settings.gradle.kts
dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositories {
        google()
        mavenCentral()
    }
    versionCatalogs {
        create("libs") { from(files("../gradle/libs.versions.toml")) }
    }
}
rootProject.name = "build-logic"
include(":convention")

The convention module is a Kotlin DSL plugin project. It puts the Android, Kotlin and KSP Gradle plugins on its classpath as compileOnly dependencies, so it can reference their types without forcing versions on the main build, and registers each plugin under an ID:

// build-logic/convention/build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    `kotlin-dsl`
}

dependencies {
    compileOnly(libs.android.gradlePlugin)
    compileOnly(libs.kotlin.gradlePlugin)
    compileOnly(libs.compose.gradlePlugin)
    compileOnly(libs.ksp.gradlePlugin)
}

gradlePlugin {
    plugins {
        register("androidLibrary") {
            id = "myapp.android.library"
            implementationClass = "AndroidLibraryConventionPlugin"
        }
        register("androidFeature") {
            id = "myapp.android.feature"
            implementationClass = "AndroidFeatureConventionPlugin"
        }
        // ...one register() per plugin
    }
}

You can write a convention plugin as a precompiled script (myapp.android.library.gradle.kts, file name = plugin ID) or as a class implementing Plugin<Project>. Classes are more verbose but are ordinary Kotlin, so plugins can share helper functions.

One place for compileSdk and minSdk

The shared helper holds the project-wide Android settings:

// KotlinAndroid.kt
internal fun Project.configureKotlinAndroid(commonExtension: CommonExtension) {
    commonExtension.apply {
        compileSdk = 36
        defaultConfig.apply {
            minSdk = 26
        }
        compileOptions.apply {
            sourceCompatibility = JavaVersion.VERSION_17
            targetCompatibility = JavaVersion.VERSION_17
        }
    }
    configure<KotlinAndroidProjectExtension> {
        compilerOptions { jvmTarget = JvmTarget.JVM_17 }
    }
}

Bumping compileSdk or minSdk is now a one-line change.

Note the shape: CommonExtension has no type arguments, and blocks are reached as properties (defaultConfig.apply { }) rather than lambdas. That is an AGP 9 change. The AGP 9.0 release notes state that the parameterization of CommonExtension was removed and the block methods moved to ApplicationExtension and LibraryExtension. Convention plugins written for AGP 8 used CommonExtension<*, *, *, *, *, *> and defaultConfig { }, and need this update when you move to AGP 9.

A tiny extension gives every plugin the version catalog:

val Project.libs: VersionCatalog
    get() = extensions.getByType<VersionCatalogsExtension>().named("libs")

The plugins themselves

An Android library:

class AndroidLibraryConventionPlugin : Plugin<Project> {
    override fun apply(target: Project) = with(target) {
        apply(plugin = "com.android.library")
        extensions.configure<LibraryExtension> {
            configureKotlinAndroid(this)
            defaultConfig.testInstrumentationRunner =
                "androidx.test.runner.AndroidJUnitRunner"
        }
        dependencies {
            "testImplementation"(libs.findLibrary("junit").get())
            "testImplementation"(libs.findLibrary("kotlinx.coroutines.test").get())
        }
    }
}

There is no Kotlin Android plugin to apply: AGP 9's built-in Kotlin support compiles the sources.

Hilt, in the style of Now in Android's HiltConventionPlugin:

class HiltConventionPlugin : Plugin<Project> {
    override fun apply(target: Project) = with(target) {
        apply(plugin = "com.google.devtools.ksp")
        pluginManager.withPlugin("org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm") {
            dependencies {
                "implementation"(libs.findLibrary("hilt.core").get())
                "ksp"(libs.findLibrary("hilt.compiler").get())
            }
        }
        pluginManager.withPlugin("com.android.base") {
            apply(plugin = "com.google.dagger.hilt.android")
            dependencies {
                "implementation"(libs.findLibrary("hilt.android").get())
                "ksp"(libs.findLibrary("hilt.android.compiler").get())
            }
        }
    }
}

pluginManager.withPlugin runs its block only if that plugin is applied, so one convention plugin serves both pure Kotlin and Android modules.

The feature plugin encodes your module rules in one place: it stacks the Compose library and Hilt plugins and adds what every feature needs.

class AndroidFeatureConventionPlugin : Plugin<Project> {
    override fun apply(target: Project) = with(target) {
        apply(plugin = "myapp.android.library.compose")
        apply(plugin = "myapp.hilt")
        dependencies {
            "implementation"(project(":core:data"))
            "implementation"(project(":core:designsystem"))
            "implementation"(project(":core:ui"))
            "testImplementation"(project(":core:testing"))
        }
    }
}

What a module's build file looks like now

// feature/notes/build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    alias(libs.plugins.myapp.android.feature)
}
android {
    namespace = "com.example.myapp.feature.notes"
}
dependencies {
    implementation(projects.core.domain)
}

Everything a feature always needs comes from the plugin; the module lists only what is special about it.

The version catalog

gradle/libs.versions.toml is where Gradle looks by default for dependency versions. It has four sections: [versions], [libraries], [bundles] for groups of libraries always used together, and [plugins] for Gradle plugin IDs. Your convention plugins get [plugins] entries too, without versions, because they come from the included build:

[plugins]
android-library = { id = "com.android.library", version.ref = "agp" }
ksp = { id = "com.google.devtools.ksp", version.ref = "ksp" }
myapp-android-library = { id = "myapp.android.library" }
myapp-android-feature = { id = "myapp.android.feature" }

A few rules keep the catalog useful:

  • Dashes become dots. androidx-navigation3-runtime is libs.androidx.navigation3.runtime in Kotlin, and libs.findLibrary("androidx.navigation3.runtime") inside a plugin.
  • Libraries under a BOM have no version. Compose entries take their versions from the Compose BOM, which the Compose convention plugin adds as a platform() dependency.
  • Bundles only for libraries that are always used together.
  • Versions live only in the catalog. A version string in any build.gradle.kts is a version that will be missed in the next upgrade.

Checklist

  • Shared build logic lives in a build-logic included build, not in subprojects {} or allprojects {}.
  • compileSdk, minSdk and the Java and Kotlin targets are set in exactly one place.
  • Convention plugins use AGP 9's unparameterized CommonExtension.
  • Each module's build file names its kind and lists only its own extras.
  • All versions live in gradle/libs.versions.toml, shared with build-logic.

item.title: Android reminders that actually fire: exact alarms, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and rescheduling after reboot
item.description: Which Android scheduler to use for "at this minute" versus "some time today", SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM versus USE_EXACT_ALARM on Android 14, asking for Alarms & reminders access, a fallback when it is denied, and the receiver that reschedules after a reboot or clock change.
item.content:encoded:
A reminder is a promise with a time on it. The user said "remind me at 9:00", and if the notification arrives at 9:40, or after the next reboot, or never, the promise is broken. Android gives you several ways to run code later, and each one trades precision for battery. This post picks the right one for each job and makes reminders survive the three things that kill them: Doze, reboots and permission changes.

The menu of "later"

NeedToolPrecision
Deferrable work: sync, cleanup, a daily digestWorkManagerMinutes to hours; runs when constraints allow
"Around this time"AlarmManager.set() / setAndAllowWhileIdle()Within an hour on Android 12+, unless battery saving delays it
"Within this window"AlarmManager.setWindow()Inside the window; short windows are usually stretched to 10 minutes
"At this minute", user-setsetExactAndAllowWhileIdle()Nearly exact, even in Doze; needs exact alarm access
An alarm clocksetAlarmClock()Exact; shown to the user as an upcoming alarm

Those figures come from Google's alarm documentation. For set() and setAndAllowWhileIdle(), the alarm never fires early, and on Android 12 (API 31) and higher the system fires it within one hour of the trigger time unless battery saver or Doze is in effect. For setWindow() on apps targeting Android 12+, windows under 600,000 milliseconds are typically clipped to 10 minutes.

An hour late is fine for "back up my notes overnight" and useless for "remind me before the meeting". A user-set reminder at a specific minute is exactly what exact alarms exist for.

Two permissions, very different terms

SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARMUSE_EXACT_ALARM
Granted byThe user, in "Alarms & reminders"Automatically at install
Can the user revoke it?YesNo
Who should declare itApps with a user-facing feature that needs precise timingCalendar and alarm clock apps
Google PlayAllowed for genuine precise-timing featuresRestricted by Play policy to limited use cases

Two details matter most. On Android 14 and higher, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM is no longer pre-granted to most newly installed apps that target Android 13 or higher; it starts out denied. And without the access, setExact(), setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() and setAlarmClock() throw a SecurityException.

A notes app with a reminder feature is not a calendar or an alarm clock. It should declare SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, ask for it in context, and fall back to an inexact alarm when the user says no. Declaring USE_EXACT_ALARM just to skip the question puts the Play listing at risk for a feature that works without it.

<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED" />

Asking for "Alarms & reminders"

SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM is a special app access, not a runtime permission. There is no dialog: you send the user to a settings page and check the result when they come back. Ask at the moment it matters, when the user sets a reminder for a specific time.

fun canScheduleExact(context: Context): Boolean {
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < 31) return true
    val am = context.getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)
    return am.canScheduleExactAlarms()
}

fun requestExactAlarmAccess(context: Context) {
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < 31) return
    context.startActivity(
        Intent(Settings.ACTION_REQUEST_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM,
            Uri.fromParts("package", context.packageName, null))
            .addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK)
    )
}

Explain why in your own UI first, then send the intent. One line under the time picker is enough: "Reminders may arrive up to an hour late. Allow exact reminders?" with an Allow button. If the user ignores it, the reminder is still saved and still fires, just less precisely.

When the user grants access, the system sends AlarmManager.ACTION_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED. Listen for it, call canScheduleExactAlarms() again rather than trusting the broadcast alone, and reschedule pending reminders as exact ones. The user can also revoke access at any time, and the system then cancels all of the app's future exact alarms.

Database first, alarm second

Store every reminder in your database first (note ID, trigger time, state), then schedule the alarm. The database is the source of truth; the alarm is only the wake-up call. That split is what makes rescheduling possible.

class ReminderScheduler(private val context: Context) {
    private val am = context.getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)

    fun schedule(r: Reminder) {
        val pi = firePendingIntent(r.noteId)
        val at = r.triggerAt.toEpochMilli()
        if (canScheduleExact(context)) {
            am.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, at, pi)
        } else {
            am.setWindow(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, at, 10 * 60 * 1000L, pi)
        }
    }

    fun cancel(noteId: Long) = am.cancel(firePendingIntent(noteId))

    private fun firePendingIntent(noteId: Long) = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(
        context, noteId.toInt(),
        Intent(context, ReminderFireReceiver::class.java)
            .setData("fieldnotes://note/$noteId".toUri()),
        PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE,
    )
}

RTC_WAKEUP uses wall-clock time and wakes the device, which is right for "9:00 tomorrow". For "in 20 minutes", ELAPSED_REALTIME_WAKEUP with SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() is immune to the user changing the clock. The data URI makes each reminder's PendingIntent unique, so cancel() cancels exactly one.

setExact* can still throw if access was revoked between your check and your call. Wrap the exact call in try/catch and fall back to the inexact path in the catch.

Surviving a reboot

Google's alarm documentation puts it plainly: "By default, all alarms are canceled when a device shuts down." The fix is to reschedule from your database when the system finishes booting, and also when the clock, the time zone or the exact-alarm access changes:

<receiver
    android:name=".reminders.RescheduleReceiver"
    android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED" />
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.TIME_SET" />
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.TIMEZONE_CHANGED" />
        <action android:name=
            "android.app.action.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED" />
    </intent-filter>
</receiver>

The receiver must be exported because the system sends these broadcasts, and the boot broadcast reaches your app only if the user has launched it at least once. Whatever the trigger, it does one thing: read every pending reminder and schedule it again.

class RescheduleReceiver : BroadcastReceiver() {
    override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) {
        when (intent.action) {
            Intent.ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED,
            Intent.ACTION_TIME_CHANGED,
            Intent.ACTION_TIMEZONE_CHANGED,
            AlarmManager.ACTION_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED -> Unit
            else -> return
        }
        val pending = goAsync()
        CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch {
            try {
                val app = context.applicationContext as FieldNotesApp
                val scheduler = ReminderScheduler(context)
                val now = Instant.now()
                app.reminders.pending().forEach { r ->
                    if (r.triggerAt.isBefore(now)) app.reminders.markMissed(r.noteId)
                    else scheduler.schedule(r)
                }
            } finally {
                pending.finish()
            }
        }
    }
}

One trap: the action string for a clock change is android.intent.action.TIME_SET, and the Kotlin constant that holds it is Intent.ACTION_TIME_CHANGED. The names differ, which catches people out. Reminders whose time passed while the phone was off are marked missed and shown in the app rather than fired late.

Testing the denied path

On an emulator, turn the app's access off in Settings, Apps, Special app access, Alarms & reminders. The app should fall back to inexact alarms and show its one-line explanation, and canScheduleExactAlarms() should report false. Then reboot the emulator and confirm pending reminders were rescheduled.

Checklist

  • Each job uses the least precise scheduler that still keeps its promise.
  • SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM is requested in context, never USE_EXACT_ALARM for a non-calendar app.
  • Reminders are stored first and scheduled second.
  • Exact calls are wrapped in try/catch with an inexact fallback.
  • A receiver reschedules on boot, clock, time zone and access changes.

Privacy and control

Is it for you?

  • You text a lot and want reply suggestions that run on your phone.

item.title: Watchtower is archived: pin your tags, get notified with Diun, update on purpose
item.description: The auto-updater most homelabs relied on is no longer maintained. Here is the safer habit from Containers Without the Chaos - pinned image tags, Diun notifications, and a six-step update routine with a rollback built in.
item.content:encoded:
For years, the default answer to "how do I keep my containers updated?" was Watchtower: run one more container and it replaces the others whenever a new image appears. That answer has expired. The Watchtower GitHub repository (containrrr/watchtower) was archived by its owner on December 17, 2025, and its README says the project is no longer maintained. Containers Without the Chaos puts it plainly: do not build a new setup on it.

That is a good moment to look at the whole update question again, because blind auto-updating was never the best fit for a homelab in the first place.

The trap: two opposite ways to get updates wrong

The book names two common traps, and they pull in opposite directions.

  • Never updating. Images that nobody touches run known vulnerabilities for years.
  • Updating blindly. An automatic updater pulls latest at 4 a.m., a breaking release arrives while you sleep, and you find out when the family does.

There is a quieter version of the second trap too: thinking you have pinned something when you have not. The tag latest is just a name. docker compose pull fetches whatever it points to today. The book calls this out as a common mistake: pinning latest and calling it pinned.

Step 1: pin tags you can reason about

An image reference can be loose or exact. The book lays out the options:

PinExampleWhat it means
Latestapp:latestWhatever the project pushed most recently
Majorapp:2Updates within version 2; usually safe
Minorapp:2.4Bug fixes only, if the project tags that way
Exactapp:2.4.1Never changes; you decide when to move
Digestapp@sha256:...Byte-for-byte the same image, forever

For anything the family relies on, pin an exact version or at least a major version, and move it on purpose. latest is fine for throwaway experiments.

The book's tip makes the exact pin painless: put the version in the stack's .env file and reference it from compose.yaml.

# .env
NOTES_VERSION=2.4.1
services:
  notes:
    image: ghcr.io/example/notes:${NOTES_VERSION}

Compose reads .env in the project folder automatically. An upgrade is now a one-line change you can see in a diff.

Step 2: get told, don't get surprised

The book compares three approaches:

ApproachHowFits
Manualdocker compose pull then up -dEverything; you choose when
AutomaticA tool replaces containers on its ownLow-risk apps only
NotifyA tool tells you; you update by handThe sweet spot

Notify is the one it recommends for a homelab. The tool it uses is Diun (Docker Image Update Notifier). Diun watches the images your containers use and tells you when a new tag or digest appears. It changes nothing; you stay in charge.

Here is the book's stack for it:

name: diun

services:
  diun:
    image: crazymax/diun:4
    command: serve
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./data:/data
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
    environment:
      TZ: ${TZ}
      DIUN_WATCH_SCHEDULE: "0 */6 * * *"
      DIUN_PROVIDERS_DOCKER: "true"
      DIUN_PROVIDERS_DOCKER_WATCHBYDEFAULT: "true"
      DIUN_NOTIF_NTFY_ENDPOINT: https://ntfy.home.example.com
      DIUN_NOTIF_NTFY_TOPIC: diun

What the settings do:

  • The schedule checks every six hours.
  • watchByDefault watches every container. Set it to false and add the label diun.enable=true only to the containers you care about, if you want a quieter feed.
  • The notification target here is ntfy, which pushes to your phone. Diun can also notify email, Gotify, Matrix, Telegram and webhooks, among others.

Each environment variable maps to a documented Diun setting (watch.schedule, providers.docker.watchByDefault, notif.ntfy.endpoint, notif.ntfy.topic). If you prefer, a YAML file (diun.yml) works too; Diun's docs list both forms for every option.

One caution from the book's Docker install chapter applies here: anything that can talk to /var/run/docker.sock controls the host, and that includes update tools. Mount it read-only where the tool allows it, as above, and only into tools you trust.

Step 3: the update routine

When a notification arrives, update one stack at a time. The book's loop is read, pull, recreate, check, and keep the old tag for rollback:

  1. Read the release notes for the new version. Look for "breaking", "migration" and "manual steps".
  2. Take a backup or a Proxmox snapshot of the VM if the app holds data you care about.
  3. Change the tag in .env, for example NOTES_VERSION=2.5.0.
  4. Pull and recreate: docker compose pull && docker compose up -d.
  5. Check: docker compose ps shows healthy, the logs are quiet, the app works.
  6. Roll back if it doesn't: put the old tag back in .env and run docker compose up -d again. Database migrations may not go backwards; that is what step 2 is for.

Because the version lives in one line of .env, steps 3 and 6 are the same edit in opposite directions.

Databases are the exception

Major database upgrades (PostgreSQL 16 to 17, for example) usually need a dump and restore, not just a new tag. The image's documentation says what is required. Pin the database's major version and upgrade it on purpose, separately from the app.

Clean up, but not too early

Old images pile up. The book's commands:

docker image prune
docker system df

docker image prune removes dangling images. Adding -a removes every image not used by a container, which also deletes the old version you might want to roll back to. Run it only after the new version has proven itself.

Checklist

  • Nothing new depends on Watchtower
  • No image the family relies on runs on latest
  • Image versions live in each stack's .env and compose.yaml references them
  • Diun (or another notifier) reports new image versions to your phone
  • The Docker socket is mounted read-only into Diun
  • Before an update: release notes read, backup or snapshot taken
  • After an update: docker compose ps healthy, logs quiet, app works
  • Databases pinned to a major version and upgraded separately
  • docker image prune -a only after the new version has proven itself

The result is the opposite of both traps: nothing runs for years untouched, and nothing changes at 4 a.m. without you. Updates become a short, boring routine you run when you choose, which is exactly what a homelab host should be.

item.title: Podcast, episode 3: The light that ignored me — automations that just work
item.description: Episode 3 of the Homelab the Right Way Podcast, 30 minutes with three AI hosts on Home Assistant's second six months: local first, Zigbee that stays up, automations that mean something, notifications nobody mutes and a one-minute update routine, plus this week's tech news, the Pantry Tracker app and a Zigbee coordinator gear break. Player, chapters, sources and links.
item.content:encoded:
Episode 3 is the Home Assistant episode. Maya, Sam and Theo work through Automations That Just Work (book 6), the book about the second six months: the house that was magic on the first weekend and that the family stopped trusting by spring. It starts with a hallway light that turned off on Theo while he was standing in it, and ends with a freezer that nobody heard about.

A note on the hosts: Maya, Sam and Theo are fictional AI hosts. Their voices are synthetic, their faces in the clips are generated, and the episode was written with AI and edited by a human. Every technical fact in the episode comes from the Homelab the Right Way books; the news segment cites its sources below.

Chapters

  • 00:04 — Cold open: the hallway light that leaves you in the dark, and welcome
  • 01:38 — New tech this week: PHP's critical fix, OpenBSD 8.0, Everything Smart Home joins Works with Home Assistant
  • 04:58 — A home that works when the internet doesn't: local first, and one naming scheme forever
  • 08:55 — Zigbee that stays up: the USB 3 trap, channels on purpose, and routers in the right places
  • 14:03 — Automations that mean something: the sentence, the mode, and the motion light done properly
  • 19:30 — App spot: Pantry Tracker
  • 20:56 — Gear break: a Zigbee coordinator, and the cable that matters more
  • 21:41 — Listener question: my family muted the house. How do I make notifications people don't ignore?
  • 25:28 — Merch, the ebooks, and the free weekly email
  • 26:54 — Update night without the panic, three takeaways, and where everything lives

New tech this week, with sources (01:38)

Three stories and a quick one, all checked the week of recording. The hosts only say what the sources say.

  • PHP: "Critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, update now" (October 21). PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical bugs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. The PHP team says every installation serving web requests is at risk and rates mod_php highest, with a demonstrated exploit that fires before any application code runs. On October 23 it added an informational advisory suggesting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release. Self-Host Weekly reports the bugs leaked ahead of the planned patches and advises updating PHP-based self-hosted apps (and Unraid) as soon as possible. Sources: php.net news archive, php.net, Self-Host Weekly, October 23.
  • OpenBSD 8.0 (October 20), the 61st OpenBSD release. Highlights per Self-Host Weekly: new GPU support, ARM64 hibernation support and wireless network driver improvements. Sources: the OpenBSD 8.0 page, Self-Host Weekly.
  • Everything Smart Home joins Works with Home Assistant (October 27). The family business founded by YouTuber Lewis Barclay and his dad Dave brings the Everything Presence Lite, One and Pro into the program. All three run ESPHome, talk to Home Assistant over the local network with no cloud connection, and carry the Made for ESPHome badge. Source: the Home Assistant blog.
  • Quick one: Linus Torvalds made his first known AI-assisted contribution to the Linux kernel, per Self-Host Weekly, October 23.

What the episode covers

A home that works when the internet doesn't (book 6, chapter 1). Prefer local push, then local polling, then cloud (fine for weather or a car, a liability for lights and locks). The integration page says which one each integration is, a ten-minute audit. The five-minute WAN unplug test: what keeps working is on solid ground, what stops goes on a replace-or-reflash list (ESPHome, Tasmota). One naming scheme forever, area then thing then measure (light.hallway_ceiling, binary_sensor.hallway_motion), renamed at the device level, never by brand or model. Every device in an area, plus labels like battery.

Zigbee that stays up (chapter 2). The three causes of an unreliable network: coordinator placement, channel, and too few routers. USB 3.0 ports and cables radiate noise in 2.4 GHz, so the stick goes on a 1 to 2 metre USB 2.0 extension cable, a metre from SSDs, hubs and access points. Coordinators from the book's table (Home Assistant Connect ZBT-1, Sonoff ZBDongle-E and -P, SMLIGHT SLZB-06 as the network pick for a Proxmox homelab). ZHA or Zigbee2MQTT: pick once and stay. Wi-Fi on 1/6/11, Zigbee on 15 or 20 (25 with caveats), set before pairing. Only mains devices route; pair routers first and pair everything in place. permit_join: false, finish every interview, check the coordinator backup exists.

Automations that mean something (chapter 4). An automation is a sentence: triggers, conditions (checked once, ANDed), actions. The four modes and why the default, single, made Theo's light ignore him. The motion light done properly: mode: restart with a wait_for_trigger for motion off for two minutes, a timer helper so it doesn't fight the wall switch, 15% brightness after 23:00 in one choose block. for: on flappy sensors, never a state trigger without to:, helpers instead of side-effect conditions, and traces: which of four things happened, read before you change anything.

Listener question: my family muted the house (chapter 7). Three kinds of notification (needs a decision now, needs attention today, nice to know) and everything else is a log entry. tag so repeats replace themselves, channel so each phone picks the volume, an actionable garage notification with a wait and a timeout and unique action names, one daily battery list (filter with is_number first), quiet hours as a schedule helper, and the alert integration for the freezer door.

The update routine (chapter 8), in one minute. Read the breaking changes, wait for the .1 or .2, back up and take a Proxmox snapshot, update one layer at a time, and roll back instead of fixing forward at 11 PM.

App spot: Pantry Tracker (19:30)

One of Charles's Android apps, free on Google Play: barcode scan or manual entry for fridge, freezer and pantry, expiry alerts with 1, 3 or 7 days' notice and a home-screen widget, and a shopping list built from low-stock and expiring items. Pro adds receipt import (on-device text recognition, you approve every line) and household sharing by file with no server and no account; the free tier has a small banner ad. Pantry Tracker on Google Play.

Gear break (20:56)

  • SONOFF ZBDongle-E Zigbee USB coordinator (we may earn a commission). The book lists it as the same chip family as the ZBT-1 and a solid budget choice. Put it on a USB 2.0 extension cable.

As an Amazon Associate the show earns from qualifying purchases.

The book, the merch and the free weekly email

The podcast merch (The Green Check Lies tee, Go Restore Something hoodie and more) is at homelab-the-right-way.printful.me. And the free weekly email arrives every Sunday with the week's posts, videos, the episode and one tip.

item.title: Provision: on-device AI meal plans with real grocery prices
item.description: Provision builds a 7-day meal plan on your phone for your diet and budget, with an itemized grocery list priced from real store data.
item.content:encoded:
Meal planning tends to break down at the grocery store. A recipe app gives you a week of dinners, then the receipt comes in well over what you meant to spend. Provision ties the two together: it plans a week of meals within a weekly budget, then prices the grocery list using real store data instead of a flat guess.

What it does

  • A full week, planned on your phone. A 7-day meal plan generated on the device, tailored to your dietary preference and weekly budget.
  • Automatic grocery list. An itemized list built from the ingredients in your plan.
  • Real prices. Live Kroger catalog prices where available, and crowdsourced real-world prices otherwise.
  • Budget tracker. See where the week's spending goes, broken down by category.
  • Cook mode. Step-by-step instructions for each recipe.
  • Five languages. English, Spanish, French, German and Portuguese, with on-device translation of every generated recipe.
  • Optional sync. Move your plan and preferences to a new phone.

How the budget works

You pick your preferred store from Kroger, Safeway, Walmart, Whole Foods or ALDI, then set a weekly budget. Provision keeps each generated plan within about $5 of that number, and if a plan comes in over, it regenerates automatically.

The prices come from two places: Kroger's public catalog where it has the item, and the free, community-run Open Prices database otherwise. Real shelf prices change and vary by location, so treat the total as a close estimate and check the receipt against the budget tracker after you shop.

A weekly routine

  1. Choose your store and your dietary preference.
  2. Set a weekly budget.
  3. Generate the 7-day plan, and regenerate if you want different meals.
  4. Shop from the itemized grocery list.
  5. Cook with step-by-step cook mode.
  6. Watch the budget tracker to see which categories take most of the money.

Privacy

The meal planner runs on your phone using Google's Gemma on-device model. According to the listing:

  • No account is required, and there is no server round-trip to make a plan.
  • Nothing about what you eat leaves your phone unless you turn on sync.
  • Price lookups go only to Kroger's public service and the Open Prices database, never to an ad network or data broker.
  • Sync, if you enable it, stores only your own preferences and plan under an anonymous account.

Good to know

  • Provision is free to use with no subscription.
  • It shows a small banner ad on the grocery list screen, and an occasional ad may appear when you manually regenerate a plan.
  • Live catalog prices are only available where Kroger has the item; other prices are crowdsourced.
  • The plan aims for your budget, but your actual spend depends on your store, location and what you add.
  • It is rated Everyone, in the Food and Drink category.

Is it for you?

  • You want a week of meals planned around a set grocery budget.
  • You shop at Kroger, Safeway, Walmart, Whole Foods or ALDI.
  • You like a grocery list that builds itself from the plan.
  • You would rather not create an account or send your eating habits to a server.

item.title: Morrowkept: a private audio journal with on-device transcripts
item.description: Morrowkept records your voice journal, transcribes it with on-device Whisper, summarizes it with local AI, and can record from a Wear OS watch.
item.content:encoded:
Talking is faster than typing, which makes a voice journal easy to keep. Finding something you said three weeks ago is another matter: audio is hard to skim. Morrowkept solves that by transcribing every recording on your phone, making it searchable, and adding AI summaries, while keeping the audio, the text and the insights on your device.

What it does

  • On-device speech-to-text. Recordings are transcribed on the phone using Whisper models, with no cloud servers, no third-party transcription services and no audio uploads.
  • Tap to jump. Tap any part of a transcript to jump straight to that moment in the audio.

item.title: Dreamloom: a private dream journal with on-device AI insights
item.description: Dreamloom lets you record dreams by voice or text, then uses on-device AI to find symbols, moods and recurring patterns. Nothing leaves your phone.
item.content:encoded:
Dreams fade fast. Within minutes of waking, most of the details are gone, and the ones you remember rarely connect to last week's. A dream journal fixes the first problem, and patterns over time handle the second. Dreamloom does both, with an AI that runs on your phone so your dreams are never sent to the cloud.

What it does

  • Quick capture. Record a dream instantly by voice or by typing.
  • Symbols and themes. On-device AI picks out the symbols and themes in each entry.
  • Tags and mood. Tag dreams and track the mood that came with them.
  • Calendar view. See your dream history laid out by date.
  • Weekly insights. Symbol analysis, weekly pattern detection and emotional tone analysis, all processed locally.
  • Reports and trends. Weekly and monthly dream reports, a recurring symbol tracker, sleep quality correlation and a visual dream timeline.

Capture first, analyze later

The most important habit in any dream journal is getting the dream down before it disappears. That is why voice entry matters: you can talk into your phone half-awake, without hunting for the right words on a keyboard. Add a mood and a tag or two if you can, and leave the rest for later.

The analysis is where Dreamloom earns its place. After a week or two of entries, the patterns start to mean something:

  • The recurring symbol tracker shows what keeps coming back.
  • Weekly pattern detection and the reports summarize what changed.
  • Emotional tone analysis shows whether your dreams have been calm or tense lately.
  • Sleep quality correlation puts your dreams next to how well you slept.

A simple routine

  1. Keep your phone within reach of the bed.
  2. When you wake up, record a voice entry right away.
  3. Add a mood and any tags that fit.
  4. Once a week, read the weekly report and the recurring symbols.
  5. Once a month, look at the timeline to see the bigger picture.

Built for late nights

The interface uses a calming dark theme meant for journaling in the dark, so opening the app at 4 a.m. will not blind you. The listing describes it as fast and easy to use, which matters most when you are barely awake.

Privacy

Dream entries are about as personal as notes get, and Dreamloom's listing is direct about how they are handled:

  • Dreams never leave your device.
  • There is no cloud sync and no account.
  • Backup is optional and local only.

Since there is no cloud copy, use the local backup option if you do not want to lose your journal when you change phones.

Good to know

  • Dreamloom is free to download, described as free with optional premium.
  • Google Play marks the app as containing ads.
  • The AI insights are interpretations to help you reflect, not a diagnosis of anything. Talk to a professional if your sleep or dreams are troubling you.
  • It is rated Everyone, in the Lifestyle category.

Is it for you?

  • You wake up with vivid dreams and lose them by breakfast.
  • You want to spot recurring symbols and moods over weeks, not just log entries.
  • You prefer speaking an entry over typing it.
  • You want your journal to stay on your phone, with no account.

item.title: Proxmox VE 9 high availability: HA rules, fencing and a failover you have actually tested
item.description: Proxmox VE HA restarts a dead node's guests elsewhere, but only on a cluster that is ready for it. How the CRM, LRM and watchdog fence a node, the new node and resource affinity rules that replaced HA groups in Proxmox VE 9, the shutdown policy, maintenance mode, and a pulled-power test.
item.content:encoded:
High availability is the feature most people build a Proxmox VE cluster for: a node dies at 3 a.m. and its important guests are running again on another node before anyone wakes up. Proxmox VE does this with two daemons, a watchdog and a set of rules. This post explains how those pieces fit together, adds guests to HA, writes placement rules (which changed in Proxmox VE 9), walks through a node failure step by step, and covers planned shutdowns and maintenance.

The trap

HA gets switched on for a cluster that is not ready for it: two nodes and no QDevice, or guests whose disks live on local storage with no replica. When a node fails, nothing restarts, or the surviving node fences itself.

The second trap is using HA as a substitute for backups. HA restarts the guest. It does not undo whatever was wrong with it.

The documented requirements are short: at least three cluster nodes (or two plus a QDevice) for reliable quorum, shared storage for the guests (or replicated storage, with a data-loss window back to the last replica), hardware redundancy, and a watchdog.

The HA stack in two daemons

Every node runs:

  • pve-ha-lrm, the local resource manager. It starts and stops HA guests on its own node, following the state the CRM requests.
  • pve-ha-crm, the cluster resource manager. One node's CRM is the active master at any time. It tells the LRMs what to run, moves guests when something fails and handles fencing.

Both rely on locks in the cluster file system and on a watchdog. While a node is healthy and quorate, its daemons keep resetting the watchdog timer. If the node loses quorum or the HA daemons stop working, the timer runs out and the watchdog resets the node.

Why fencing matters

Before a guest from a failed node can start somewhere else, the cluster must be certain the failed node is not still running it, perhaps cut off from the network but still writing to shared storage. Starting a second copy would corrupt the disk. Making sure the node is really off is called fencing.

Proxmox VE fences with watchdog timers. A node outside the quorate part of the cluster cannot reset its watchdog, so the watchdog resets it. Once the CRM master can take the failed node's lock, it knows the node has fenced itself and can recover its guests.

Without a configured hardware watchdog, Proxmox VE uses the Linux kernel's softdog, which the docs describe as reliable but not independent of the server's hardware. Hardware watchdog modules are blocked by default; to use one, name its module and reboot:

# /etc/default/pve-ha-manager
WATCHDOG_MODULE=iTCO_wdt

One warning from the docs worth repeating: never kill pve-ha-crm, pve-ha-lrm or watchdog-mux by hand. They manage the watchdog, and killing them can cause an immediate reset of the node.

Adding guests to HA

An HA resource is a type and an ID: vm:100, ct:110.

ha-manager add vm:100
ha-manager add ct:110 --state started --max_restart 1 --max_relocate 1
ha-manager config
ha-manager status

In the web interface it is Datacenter → HA → Resources → Add, or More → Manage HA on a guest.

--state is the requested state: started, stopped, disabled or ignored. Once HA manages a guest, ordinary qm start and qm stop simply change its requested state. max_restart is how often HA retries starting it on the same node after a failed start, and max_relocate how often it tries another node; both default to 1.

ha-manager set vm:100 --state stopped     # stop and keep stopped
ha-manager migrate vm:100 pve2            # live migration
ha-manager relocate vm:100 pve2           # stop, move, start
ha-manager remove vm:100                  # stop managing (does not stop it)

Before you add a guest, check it can run on every node HA might pick: disks on shared or replicated storage, bridges with the same names on every node, and no passthrough devices. If a dependency exists on only some nodes, restrict the guest to them with a strict node affinity rule.

HA groups became HA rules in Proxmox VE 9

Earlier releases used HA groups to say which nodes a guest prefers. Proxmox VE 9.0 deprecated them in favour of HA rules, stored in /etc/pve/ha/rules.cfg. Existing groups are migrated to node affinity rules automatically once every node runs Proxmox VE 9; if anything looks wrong afterwards, the upgrade guide points to the active CRM's log, journalctl -eu pve-ha-crm.

Node affinity: which nodes a guest runs on

# Prefer pve1 for the firewall VM; any node is fine if pve1 is down
ha-manager rules add node-affinity fw-on-pve1 --resources vm:100 \
  --nodes pve1
# Make it a hard requirement instead
ha-manager rules set node-affinity fw-on-pve1 --strict 1
# Ordered preference: pve1 first, then pve2 or pve3 equally
ha-manager rules add node-affinity ha-core \
  --resources vm:101,ct:110 --nodes "pve1:2,pve2:1,pve3:1"
# Keep these guests off pve3 (the small node)
ha-manager rules add node-affinity not-pve3 --affinity negative \
  --resources ct:200,vm:300 --nodes pve3

Node affinity rules are not strict by default: if none of the listed nodes is available, the guest may run elsewhere. With --strict 1 it is restricted to the listed nodes and stopped if none of them is up. Priorities are relative; higher numbers win, and nodes without a number get 0. failback, a per-resource property that defaults to on, moves a guest back to its highest-priority node when that node returns.

Resource affinity: guests together or apart

# Two DNS servers should never share a node
ha-manager rules add resource-affinity dns-apart --affinity negative \
  --resources ct:120,ct:121
# An app and its database should stay together
ha-manager rules add resource-affinity app-with-db --affinity positive \
  --resources vm:130,vm:131

Resource affinity rules are the opposite: strict by default. A negative rule cannot list more resources than there are nodes.

Rules are checked for conflicts before they apply. A resource can be in only one node affinity rule, for example, and two resources cannot be kept both together and apart. A conflicting rule is disabled until you resolve it, so run ha-manager rules config after every edit.

What happens when a node dies

  1. Node pve2 loses power. Corosync on pve1 and pve3 stops hearing from it and forms a new membership without it. Two of three votes: still quorate.
  2. The CRM master marks pve2's HA guests as waiting for fencing (state fence).
  3. If pve2 were still running but cut off, it would be in a minority without quorum and unable to reset its watchdog, and the watchdog (60 seconds, per the docs) would reset it. A node with no power is already fenced in practice.
  4. Once the CRM can take pve2's lock, the node counts as fenced and its guests move to recovery.
  5. The CRM picks a node for each guest from the online, quorate nodes, narrowed by the affinity rules, and chooses the one with the lowest load. The guests start there.
  6. When pve2 comes back it rejoins the cluster, and guests with failback move back if a rule prefers it.

With Ceph or shared storage the guests start with every completed write intact. With ZFS replication they start from the last replica. And every guest that ran on the failed node now runs on fewer nodes, which the docs warn can overload small clusters: size each node so the others can carry its HA guests, or mark only what truly matters as HA.

Test it with the power cord

Before you trust HA with the firewall, test it with a disposable VM: add it to HA, then pull the power cord (not a clean shutdown) of the node running it. Watch ha-manager status on another node until the VM shows as started on its new home. A clean shutdown tests something else, the shutdown policy.

Planned shutdowns: pick a shutdown policy

A planned shutdown is not a failure, and HA handles it according to the cluster's shutdown policy, set in Datacenter → Options → HA Settings or in datacenter.cfg:

ha: shutdown_policy=migrate
  • conditional (the default): on shutdown, stop the guests and let other nodes take them over; on reboot, freeze them and start them again on the same node.
  • migrate: mark the node unavailable and live-migrate its HA guests away first; they return when it is back.
  • failover: stop the guests and recover them elsewhere if the node is not back soon.
  • freeze: stop and freeze the guests; nothing moves until the node returns.

The docs note that conditional is the default for backward compatibility and that some users find migrate behaves more as expected. One catch with migrate: a guest restricted by a strict node affinity rule to unavailable nodes makes the shutdown hang until you step in.

Maintenance mode for one node

For work on a single node, maintenance mode is the cleanest tool. It migrates the node's HA guests away and brings them back when you disable it:

ha-manager crm-command node-maintenance enable pve2
ha-manager status          # wait until no HA guests remain on pve2
# ... patch, reboot, replace hardware ...
ha-manager crm-command node-maintenance disable pve2

It can run from any node. The LRM shows maintenance as soon as the request is picked up, before every guest has moved, so watch the guest list rather than the status word. Maintenance mode survives a reboot and ends only when you disable it.

For work that could briefly break quorum everywhere, such as re-cabling the corosync network, Proxmox VE 9.2 added a cluster-wide switch: ha-manager crm-command disarm-ha freeze, then ha-manager crm-command arm-ha when you are done. While HA is disarmed it protects nothing, so keep the window short.

Checklist

  • Quorum survives one node down (three nodes, or two plus a QDevice).
  • Every HA guest's disks are on shared, Ceph or replicated storage.
  • Every rule in ha-manager rules config is enabled (no conflicts).
  • The shutdown policy is a deliberate choice, not the default by accident.
  • A pulled-power failover test of a disposable VM succeeded.
  • Each node can carry the HA guests of any one failed node.

item.title: Will this model fit on your GPU? Size a local LLM on paper before you pull it
item.description: When ollama ps shows a CPU/GPU split, your model did not fit and everything runs at the speed of system RAM. Parameters, quantization and the KV cache turn sizing into arithmetic: weights + context + overhead, worked through for Llama 3.1 8B, then checked against ollama ps.
item.content:encoded:
You download the biggest model your disk can hold, ask it a question, and wait. The answer arrives a word at a time, the CPU fans spin up, and ollama ps says 45%/55% CPU/GPU. The model did not fit in the card's memory, so part of it runs from system RAM, and the whole thing moves at the speed of that slow part. The opposite mistake is just as common: a tiny model that fits easily but cannot follow a two-step instruction.

Sizing is arithmetic, not guesswork. Three numbers decide whether a model fits: its parameters, its quantization, and the context you give it.

Parameters: what the "8b" means

A model's name usually carries its size: llama3.1:8b, qwen3:14b, gemma3:27b. The number is the parameter count in billions, the weights the model learned during training. More parameters generally means more knowledge and better reasoning, and always means more memory and slower answers on the same hardware.

At full 16-bit precision each parameter takes 2 bytes, so an 8-billion-parameter model is about 16 GB of weights. That is why the Ollama library lists llama3.1:8b-instruct-fp16 at 16 GB.

Mixture-of-experts models such as qwen3:30b or gpt-oss:20b hold all their parameters in memory but use only part of them for each word, so they can answer faster than a dense model of the same size. For sizing, what matters is the full size of the file you load.

Quantization: smaller numbers, smaller model

Quantization stores each weight with fewer bits. A model quantized to about 4 bits per weight is roughly a quarter the size of the 16-bit original, and in practice loses surprisingly little quality on most tasks. Ollama and llama.cpp use the GGUF file format, and the quantization is part of the tag:

  • Q8_0: about 8 bits per weight. Closest to the original, twice the size of Q4.
  • Q6_K, Q5_K_M: the middle ground.
  • Q4_K_M: about 4 to 5 bits per weight. The common default, and what Ollama gives you for a plain tag like llama3.1:8b.
  • Q3_K_M, Q2_K: smaller still, with a visible quality cost.
  • fp16 or bf16: no quantization at all.

Start at Q4_K_M. Move up only if you have memory to spare and can see a difference on your own prompts. Dropping to Q3 or Q2 to squeeze in a bigger model is usually worse than running a smaller model at Q4.

Context: the memory everyone forgets

The context window is how many tokens the model can see at once: the system prompt, the conversation so far, any retrieved documents and the answer it is writing. Ollama picks a default from the card's memory; its context-length page lists 4k tokens below 24 GiB of VRAM, 32k from 24 to 48 GiB and 256k at 48 GiB or more.

Context costs memory because the model keeps a KV cache: for every token in the window it stores a key and a value vector in every layer. The size per token comes straight from the model's architecture:

KV bytes per token = 2 (key and value) x layers x KV heads x head size x bytes per number

Llama 3.1 8B's published configuration has 32 layers, 8 key-value heads and a head size of 128. With a 16-bit cache:

2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes, about 0.13 MB per token
  4,096 tokens  ->  about 0.54 GB
  8,192 tokens  ->  about 1.07 GB
 32,768 tokens  ->  about 4.29 GB
131,072 tokens  ->  about 17.2 GB

That last line is the full context Llama 3.1 supports, and its cache alone is bigger than the 16-bit model. Long context is not free.

Two settings change the picture. Ollama can store the cache in 8-bit numbers: its FAQ lists f16 as the default, q8_0 as about half the memory with a very small loss in precision, and q4_0 as smaller still with a more noticeable loss. A quantized cache needs flash attention, which Ollama enables automatically where the hardware supports it. And parallel requests multiply context: with OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4, the FAQ says required memory scales with the number of parallel requests times the context length, so four parallel 8K conversations reserve as much cache as one 32K conversation.

The estimate

Add three things:

  1. Weights: the file size of the tag you pull.
  2. KV cache: per-token size times context length (times parallel requests).
  3. Overhead: compute buffers, the CUDA runtime and whatever else sits on the card. It varies by model, backend and driver; the examples below assume about 1 GB, and you confirm the real number on your own machine.

Llama 3.1 8B with an 8,192-token context, using the library's file sizes. These are estimates, rounded to a tenth of a gigabyte:

TagWeightsKV cache (8K, f16)Overhead (assumed)Estimate
8b-instruct-q4_K_M4.9 GB1.1 GB1.0 GBabout 7.0 GB
8b-instruct-q5_K_M5.7 GB1.1 GB1.0 GBabout 7.8 GB
8b-instruct-q8_08.5 GB1.1 GB1.0 GBabout 10.6 GB
8b-instruct-fp1616 GB1.1 GB1.0 GBabout 18.1 GB

The same model at Q4_K_M as the context grows:

ContextKV cacheEstimate (f16 cache)Estimate (q8_0 cache)
4,0960.5 GBabout 6.4 GBabout 6.2 GB
8,1921.1 GBabout 7.0 GBabout 6.4 GB
32,7684.3 GBabout 10.2 GBabout 8.0 GB

Read the tables against your card. An 8 GB card runs the Q4_K_M model comfortably at the default context and gets tight at 8K. A 12 GB card has room for 8K at Q5_K_M, or 32K with a quantized cache. A 16 GB card can hold Q8_0 at 8K. Leave a margin: if the estimate is within a gigabyte of the card's total, expect Ollama to spill part of the model to system RAM.

Check it against reality

An estimate is a starting point. Load the model with the context you plan to use, then:

ollama ps

The SIZE column is what Ollama actually allocated, the CONTEXT column is the context it used, and the PROCESSOR column must say 100% GPU. If it shows a CPU/GPU split, pick a smaller quantization, a smaller context or a smaller model, and check again.

Picking the file

The Ollama library at ollama.com/library lists every model's sizes, context window and capabilities, and each tags page lists every quantization with its file size. ollama pull qwen3:8b downloads the default quantization; ollama pull llama3.1:8b-instruct-q5_K_M asks for a specific one.

Hugging Face hosts many more GGUF files, and Ollama can run them directly:

# Q4_K_M is used by default when the repository has it
ollama run hf.co/bartowski/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-GGUF

# Ask for a specific quantization by its tag
ollama run hf.co/bartowski/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-GGUF:Q8_0

Stick to repositories from the model's publisher or well-known quantizers, and read the model card, including the license, before you build anything on top. "Open" models come with very different licenses: as listed on Hugging Face in October 2026, Llama 3.1 uses the Llama 3.1 Community License and Gemma 3 the Gemma Terms of Use, while Qwen3, gpt-oss and Mistral 7B are Apache 2.0.

Checklist

  • You know your card's memory before you pick a model.
  • You start at Q4_K_M and move up only with memory to spare.
  • You estimate weights + KV cache + overhead before you pull.
  • You know the context you need, and that parallel requests multiply it.
  • ollama ps shows the SIZE you expected and 100% GPU after loading.
  • You have read the license of every model you build on.
